The Foundations

The map the rest stands on — gunas, prana and the sheaths, and Tantra’s one move

The Three Gunas

The weather of the mind

Ayurveda and Samkhya+Sanskrit, “enumeration.” One of the six classical schools of Indian philosophy. It describes reality as pure awareness (Purusha) and nature (Prakriti) unfolding through the three gunas into mind, body and elements — the groundwork Ayurveda draws on. describe all of nature, including mental states, as a shifting mixture of three qualities: Sattva (clarity, balance), Rajas (activity, restlessness), and Tamas (inertia, dullness). None is "bad" — they're weather, not character. The work is noticing which one is currently running the show.

The word guna literally means a strand or cord. The image behind it is three strands twisted into one rope, and the Gita+The Bhagavad Gita, a dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna set within the Mahabharata. References like (14.5) mean chapter 14, verse 5. Not the Ashtavakra Gita glossed elsewhere on this site. says these three strands bind the embodied self to the body (14.5). Binding is not a verdict: even sattva binds, through attachment to its own happiness and knowledge (14.6). So the work is noticing which strand is pulling, not collecting the “good” one.

Word-trap: this rope is not the rope mistaken for a snake in the illustration of superimposition (Adhyasa). That rope is a misread object; this one is a binding.

Sattva

Clear, light, undistorted

Rajas

Driven, agitated, grasping

Tamas

Heavy, dull, resistant

Prana as the Bridge

Where breath meets attention, and which sheaths it works

Prana+Life-force or vital energy; also refers specifically to the inhaled breath in yogic anatomy. is the working link Yoga uses between body and mind that Vedanta's pure inquiry mostly leaves untouched. Breath is the one autonomic process you can also run manually — which makes it the practical door into the gap between trigger and reaction that the RRRR Protocol names conceptually.

The seven-level model of existence already on this site has a companion in Vedanta's five koshas+Sanskrit: sheaths or coverings. Vedanta describes the self as five nested layers, from the dense physical body inward to bliss: annamaya, pranamaya, manomaya, vijnanamaya, anandamaya. (sheaths) — annamaya (physical), pranamaya (energetic), manomaya (mental), vijnanamaya (wisdom), anandamaya (bliss). Yoga's asana and pranayama practices work primarily on the first two sheaths — not as an end in themselves, but as the ground floor that has to be reasonably stable before subtler work holds.

Where RRRR asks you to notice the gap, pranayama gives you a lever to physically widen it. Next: how this link breaks down, in Two Kinds of Illness, and later how breath reaches the fire, in The Bellows.

Tantra's Reframe: Nothing to Reject

Transmutation over renunciation

Where some ascetic paths treat the body and senses as obstacles to transcend, Tantra's central move is different: nothing is excluded from the path. Desire, anger, and pleasure aren't enemies to suppress — they're energy to be recognized and redirected, the same way the Pain-Body section already describes turning attention itself into the transmuting agent.

This is offered as a lens, not a practice prescription — *SELF doesn't teach Tantric ritual, only borrows its core insight: what you resist, persists; what you include, transforms.

The Body Is Not the Enemy

How the physicians’ tradition pushed back on body-denial

Traditional Source

“Tantra’s Reframe” is a lens. Ayurveda carries the same stance as a history. Beside currents that ranked the body below the spirit, the Vaidya+Sanskrit: physician. The classical Indian medical profession, trained in a teacher’s household and held to its own code of conduct.s held that the body is where practice happens, and that practice needs it in working order.

Two Currents

Purity and practice

The Purity Current
Rank by cleanness

Ritual purity comes first. Blood, illness and earth count as polluting, and so, by contact, does the person who handles them. The Manusmriti, the lawgiver Manu’s code, is recorded as calling a physician’s food as vile as pus, keeping physicians away from sacrifices, and barring the twice-born from practising medicine for income except in extreme need.

The Physician’s Current
Rank by what heals

The Charaka Samhita answers from the clinic. It tells physicians to claim the Atharva-Veda openly, and calls the one who completes medical study “twice-born” by initiation, putting medicine on a par with Vedic study whatever the caste. Health is also named the root of the four aims of life, the same four as in “Health Is a Form of Wealth.”

Svasthya was never a way of leaving the body behind. It is being established in the Self while living in one. The profession that said so was the one that had to touch the body to do its work.

Reflect: where do you treat your body as a delay on the real work?

What Health Means

Not the absence of disease — a direction, and a form of wealth

The Quadrant of Health

Where “not sick” stops being the finish line

Modern yoga therapy maps health as four stops on one climb, not two — and most people only ever walk between the first two.

The Four Stops

Sick man to towards divinity

I
Sick Man

Ill health. Survival only — the animal level, nothing above it.

II
Normal Man

No diagnosis, but still run by the fear of death. Where most people file “healthy” and stop looking.

III
Super Man

Wellbeing actively built — a state pursued on purpose, not just an absence nobody disturbed.

IV
Towards Divinity

Self-realization. The far edge of the same climb, not a different one.

Health was never a checkbox. It’s a direction — and most people stop reporting for duty the moment nothing hurts.

Health Is a Form of Wealth

Where the body sits among the four aims of life

Indian thought names four aims of a human life, the Purusharthas, and puts them in order. Health isn’t a separate project beside them. It sits inside the second one.

The Four Aims

Dharma, artha, kama, moksha

1 · Dharma
Foundation

The ethical ground: values and principles. Nothing above it stands without it.

2 · Artha
Wealth

Resources in four forms: knowledge, health, contentment, material wealth.

3 · Kama
Desire

Fulfilment held without gripping the outcome — desire that inspires giving and discovery.

4 · Moksha
Liberation

Pure bliss: the state of desiring nothing more.

Notice what counts as wealth: contentment is on the list, and money is meant to be mastered as energy, not served. Health, as the second rung, is part of the foundation for liberation, not a detour from it. Svasthya, again, but as an order of operations.

What is the strength for? Clean digestion becomes strength. The tradition does not stop there, and it does not answer with rest or accumulation. It answers with practice, good work, and freedom. What did yesterday’s strength go toward?

Three word-traps here. Purushartha also appears on this site as self-effort in the Destiny section, and Artha as object of the senses in the Katha map. Popular summaries also narrow it a third way, to money alone; here it keeps its fuller four-form sense. Same roots, different uses; context decides.

Health Beyond the Skin

When the body, the land and the society are one patient

Traditional Source

Svasthya so far has been personal. Ayurveda’s vocabulary does not stop at the skin. It reads the person as a small copy of the world around them, so health is measured as the fit between the two.

Two Scales, One Pattern

Macrocosm and microcosm

Macrocosm
The world around

Seasons, weather, land and water, moving through their own cycles of growth, settling and release.

Microcosm
The person within

The same rhythms in compressed form. “The Body Keeps a Clock” is the working version: the doshas rise and fall with the hour and the season.

The Rain Story

Health said out loud

Field research in Sri Lanka recorded this: after a devastating drought, a woman watched the rain begin to fall and said, simply, “Look, it is health.” It was not a medical remark. It was the same word used for the body, now used for the weather, because balance restored out there is the same kind of thing as balance restored in here.

The vocabulary travels. Balance, heat, blockage and digestion get used for a stomach, a household, even a government. In that idiom a society in disorder is not like a sick person. It is sick.

This is a way of reading, not a claim that politics can be treated with herbs. What it adds to Svasthya is scale: a person cannot be fully well in isolation from what they live inside.

Reflect: what is out of balance around you that you have been counting as only your own?

The rain remark is a record of how people talk, not evidence about health.

How Illness Arises

From mind to body — two kinds of illness and the chain, the doshas and their clock, the fire and its breath, the tissues, the stages, the channels

Two Kinds of Illness

Vyadhi, traced to its address and then stage by stage

Patanjali named illness first among the nine obstacles and moved on without saying where it actually comes from. The yoga-therapy tradition splits Vyadhi+Illness or bodily disturbance — already named earlier as the first of Patanjali's nine obstacles to practice. into two separate addresses before it ever reaches a diagnosis.

The Four Addresses

Anadhija, Adhija, Sara, Samanya

Anadhija+Illness not generated by mental agitation — infection, injury, contagion, anything arriving from outside the mind.
Not From the Mind

Infection, injury, contagion — what medicine alone was always built to treat.

Adhija+Illness generated by Adhi, mental agitation — the psychosomatic branch, traced stage by stage in “How a Thought Becomes an Ulcer.”
From the Mind

Mental agitation, translated downward until the body is the one holding it.

Sara+The essential or constitutional subtype of Adhija Vyadhi — deep-rooted, present from early on.
Deep-Rooted

Constitutional. Present early, and rarely traced to one triggering week.

Samanya+The ordinary subtype of Adhija Vyadhi — manufactured by everyday stress rather than constitution.
Ordinary

The everyday, stress-manufactured kind — what “How a Thought Becomes an Ulcer” traces stage by stage.

A cough and an ulcer can look identical on a chart. One arrived from outside. The other was built, meal by meal, thought by thought, from in here.

Prana was already named as the working link between mind and body. This is that link shown breaking down — the mechanism behind the “ordinary” illness above.

How a Thought Becomes an Ulcer

Samanya Vyadhi, traced stage by stage: Manomaya to Annamaya

Manomaya
Mind in Overdrive

Speed. Insomnia, restlessness, indecision — the mind racing fast enough to generate its own friction.

Pranamaya
Erratic Energy

The same speed forces breath haphazard, unsettling the Nadis covered a few sections back.

Digestion
Under, Over, or Wrong

Ajeernatvam+Under-digestion — too little energy to process food, leaving it stagnant., Atijeernatvam+Over-digestion — hyperactive energy burning through nourishment too quickly., or Kujeernatvam+Wrong digestion — chaotic energy digesting irregularly, generating toxins. — energy no longer metabolizes food cleanly, in one of three directions.

Annamaya
Physical Manifestation

Gastritis → tissue erosion → ulcer. Medicine treats the ulcer. It rarely asks what was racing upstream.

The Gita's own definition of the practice: samatvam yoga uchyate — equanimity is yoga. Not a pose. A speed control. The Prana bridge and the Nadi work covered earlier are the actual levers for turning the speed down before Stage 3 ever starts.

The Three Doshas

Vata, Pitta, Kapha — the body’s working patterns

Ayurveda reads body and mind through three biological energies, the doshas. They aren’t organs or substances but patterns of function, each built from two of the five elements. Don’t confuse them with the three gunas (“The Three Gunas”): the gunas are qualities of mind-nature; the doshas are how the body-mind actually runs.

The Three Profiles

Vata, Pitta, Kapha — what each governs and how it tips

Air + Ether
Vata

Governs: movement, breath, the nervous system.
Qualities: dry, light, cold, rough, mobile.
Balanced: creativity, flexibility.
Out of balance: anxiety, dry skin.

Fire + Water
Pitta

Governs: digestion, metabolism, body temperature.
Qualities: hot, sharp, light, oily, liquid.
Balanced: intelligence, strong digestion.
Out of balance: anger, inflammation.

Earth + Water
Kapha

Governs: structure, immunity, body fluids.
Qualities: heavy, slow, cool, oily, stable.
Balanced: calmness, strength.
Out of balance: lethargy, weight gain.

Everyone carries all three, in different proportions, and they shift with food, season, age, and the state of the mind. Weather, not a verdict. The “mind in overdrive” stage of “How a Thought Becomes an Ulcer” reads closest to Vata moving too fast.

These are traditional descriptions, offered as a vocabulary for noticing tendencies, not as a diagnosis or a label to wear.

The Body Keeps a Clock

Same body, different hours

Ayurveda reads the day, the year and a life as three turns of one wheel, each leaning toward a different dosha. The doshas from “The Three Doshas” aren’t fixed in you; they rise and fall with the hour.

Three Turns of One Wheel

Day, year, life

Kapha · heavy, damp
The Slow Turn

Day: morning.
Year: spring.
Life: childhood, which grows.

Pitta · hot, sharp
The Bright Turn

Day: midday, when the digestive fire peaks.
Year: summer.
Life: adulthood, which transforms.

Vata · dry, mobile
The Dry Turn

Day: late day.
Year: autumn.
Life: old age, which dries.

Advice That Follows the Hour

Why the tradition keeps a schedule

The heaviest meal when the fire is strongest. Early rising, to clear the morning’s heaviness. A slow oil massage, to give restless Vata a rhythm. Illness is said to strike at the junctures, when one season hands over to the next and the body realigns imperfectly.

Reflect: which hour of your day is hardest to digest, in the food sense or the other sense?

Traditional descriptions, offered as a vocabulary for noticing rhythm, not as medical advice.

Which Pattern Runs You?

Baseline versus right now — noticing, not testing

“The Three Profiles” says what each dosha governs. This card turns it around: what do you actually notice in yourself? The tradition separates two things — the baseline mix you were born with, Prakriti+An individual’s baseline constitution in Ayurveda — the proportion of Vata, Pitta and Kapha the tradition holds you start with. Not the Samkhya sense of “nature itself.”, and the mix you are in right now, Vikriti+Sanskrit: altered or changed. In Ayurveda, the current state of the doshas as they stand now, as distinct from the baseline (Prakriti).. The baseline is a tendency. The current state is the part that moves, and the part you can work with.

Word-trap: Prakriti here means one person’s constitution. Elsewhere on this site, in the Samkhya passages, it means nature itself. Same root, different use; context decides.

Five Things to Notice

Appetite, elimination, sleep, temperament, stress

Air + Ether
Vata

Appetite: variable, easily satisfied.
Elimination: dry, small, prone to constipation.
Sleep: light, easily interrupted.
Temperament: creative, restless, indecisive.
Under stress: anxiety and fear.

Fire + Water
Pitta

Appetite: strong, gets very hungry.
Elimination: loose, abundant.
Sleep: short but sound.
Temperament: focused, sharp, brave.
Under stress: anger and inflammation.

Earth + Water
Kapha

Appetite: steady but modest, slow to feel hungry.
Elimination: slow, heavy.
Sleep: heavy, long, hard to rouse.
Temperament: calm, steady, affectionate.
Under stress: sluggishness and holding on.

Build, hair and skin are traditionally read too. They are left out here on purpose: they are the easiest rows to turn into a label and the least useful for noticing what you actually do.

Most people see themselves in more than one column, and the answer shifts with season, age and the week you have had. For a current-state read, compare how you are this month to how you usually are. The difference is the Vikriti. The Kapha appetite line is this site’s own summary, not a classical phrase.

The Last Row Is the Gap

Stress response, read through RRRR

The last row matters most on this site. It is the reaction in trigger → gap → reaction, and each pattern tends to meet the gap differently.

Arrives fast
Vata · worry

The reaction lands as fear before you notice it. The risk: the gap closes almost at once. What steadies: a slower, longer exhale; regular wake time and meals (“The Bellows”).

Arrives hot
Pitta · verdict

The reaction lands as a judgment or a sharp word. The risk: the gap is there, but spent rehearsing the case. What cools: waiting before replying; anything cool, soft and unhurried.

Arrives heavy
Kapha · holding on

The reaction lands as withdrawal, delay or clinging. The risk: the trigger is never noticed at all. What moves it: one small, light action; naming the trigger out loud.

Pair this with the RRRR Protocol and the Pattern Test. The pairings are this site’s own synthesis, not a classical prescription: they are the rule “like increases like” applied to a reaction. Breath advice stays as on “The Bellows”: gentle only, no holding.

Reflect: when you are stressed, which of the three reactions arrives first, and how many seconds does it take?

A vocabulary for noticing tendencies, not a diagnosis or a label to wear. Persistent changes in appetite, sleep or bowels belong with a clinician, not a column.

Like Increases Like

The one rule underneath the doshas, the tastes and the remedies

The tradition sorts the world into twenty qualities in ten opposing pairs. Everything you meet, from food and weather to company and mood, carries some of them, and everything you take in tends to increase what it resembles.

Twenty Qualities

Ten opposing pairs

Guru · Laghu
Heavy · Light

A heavy meal, a heavy mood. A light broth, a clear head.

Ushna · Sheeta
Hot · Cold

Spice and irritation. Ice and aloofness.

Manda · Tikshna
Slow · Sharp

Dull, foggy thinking. A keen edge, or a cutting remark.

Snigdha · Ruksha
Oily · Dry

Warmth, tenderness. Brittleness, a dried-out mind.

Shlakshna · Khara
Smooth · Rough

An even routine. A ragged breath, a rough week.

Sandra · Drava
Dense · Liquid

Thick, stuck feeling. Fluid, flowing, hard to hold.

Mridu · Kathina
Soft · Hard

Gentleness, yielding. Rigidity, a clenched jaw.

Sthira · Chala
Stable · Mobile

A steady habit. A mind that will not sit still.

Sukshma · Sthula
Subtle · Gross

Fine perception, quick to seep in. Bulk, coarseness.

Vishada · Pichchila
Clear · Sticky

Clean-edged, easy to let go of. Clinging, hard to shake.

All ten pairs. Whatever shares a quality with you strengthens it; whatever opposes it steadies it. Read “The Three Profiles” again with this list in hand: Vata and Kapha share the cool end of Hot · Cold but sit at opposite ends of most other pairs (light and heavy, dry and oily, rough and smooth, mobile and stable), while Pitta stands apart on hot and sharp.

Two earlier tiles, Dull · Sharp and Slow · Quick, are folded into one here. In the classical list Manda (slow, dull) and Tikshna (sharp, quick-acting) are a single pair. The Sanskrit names above are the classical ones; the everyday lines are this site’s illustrations.

So a restless, dry state is not fixed with more speed, and a heavy, stuck one is not fixed with more rest. The same logic runs through the six tastes, and it is why “Six Questions Before Any Remedy” never ends in a universal formula.

Reflect: what are you feeding in yourself right now by giving it more of what it already is?

The Agni Engine

Digesting everything that arrives — and the signs of what hasn’t been

“How a Thought Becomes an Ulcer” traced how an overdriven mind ends in a gut problem. Ayurveda explains why the route exists: Agni+Digestive fire — the capacity to transform what is taken in, whether food, medicine, or experience. isn’t only the stomach’s fire. It is the transforming capacity applied to every input — food, emotions, sense impressions, experiences. What it digests cleanly becomes strength; what it doesn’t becomes weight. Behind it sits a subtler fire, tejas, and breath is how you reach both (The Bellows).

The Four Moments

Input, filter, clear, unclear

Input
What Arrives

Food, emotions, senses, experiences — all treated as things to be digested.

Filter
The Fire

Agni: metabolism, absorption, and mental processing in one function.

Clear
Ojas+Vitality — the refined essence left when digestion is clean; felt as radiance, resilience, and a rested mind.

The result of clean digestion: vigor, radiance, a rested mind.

Unclear
Ama+Undigested residue — what is left when something was taken in but not fully processed.

The result of poor digestion: heaviness, toxicity, stagnation — from unprocessed food or unresolved emotion alike.

Three States of the Fire

Smoldering, flaring, unstable — and the mood each carries

Slow · Manda
Smoldering

Weak, sluggish digestion. Mood: depression, feeling stuck and depleted. Kapha’s tendency.

Sharp · Tikshna
Flaring

Overactive, aggressive digestion. Mood: irritability, impatience. Pitta’s tendency.

Irregular · Vishama+Sanskrit: uneven or irregular. The unstable state of agni — strong one hour, weak the next — with gas, erratic digestion and anxious restlessness. Vata’s tendency.
Unstable

Gas and erratic digestion. Mood: anxiety, restlessness. Vata’s tendency. The state breath work reaches first: The Bellows.

These are the under-, over- and wrong-digestion of “How a Thought Becomes an Ulcer,” now with the mood each one carries and the dosha from “The Three Doshas” it follows. The tradition runs the chain both ways: a steadier gut steadies the mind, as a calmer mind steadies the gut.

Is Something Going Undigested?

A self-check for load, not a diagnosis

Notice how many are true this week

1
Caffeine to Start

Needing it to begin the day, not just enjoying it.

2
Foggy Waking

A heavy, foggy mind as the day opens.

3
Coated Tongue

A visible coating in the morning.

4
Blocked or Flat

A sense of blockage, or enthusiasm gone flat.

5
Re-chewing

An experience you keep going back over.

6
Heavy Stools

Stools that feel heavy and sink, rather than passing cleanly.

7
Mucus & Chest Colds

Mucus that keeps returning, or chest colds that come back often.

Several at once is information about load, not a diagnosis. The tradition’s response is simple: reduce what you take in, eat when you are actually hungry, and let one thing finish before the next arrives.

If these persist, or anything worries you, see a clinician. This is a lens for noticing, not a screening.

Unresolved emotion is as hard to digest as unprocessed food. Undigested experience reads like a close cousin of what this framework calls samskara: the residue that stays after the moment has passed.

The Bellows

How breath reaches the fire

Breath is the only part of the fire you can reach by hand. Prana moves the air; the air feeds the fire. A smooth, regular breath lets agni burn cleanly, and a gusty, broken one makes it flare or gutter. That is why the tradition teaches rhythm as medicine: a regular wake time, regular meals, regular breath.

A third partner sits behind agni: Tejas+The subtle fire in Ayurveda — the quality of attention that transforms food, emotion and ideas, and, in balance, guards ojas; too much can burn it away. Not to be confused with the elemental “tejas” in Sanatkumara’s ladder., the subtle fire that digests food, emotions and ideas, and, in balance, guards ojas. Run too hot, it can burn ojas away. Where agni is the engine, tejas is the quality of attention running it. Prana feeds it, tejas transforms what arrives, and ojas is what is left when it goes well.

The Same Chain, Two Ways

Where the breath changes the ending

When the mind runs ahead

1
Trigger

Something lands.

2
Mind speeds up

Vata rises.

3
Breath goes ragged

Gusty, broken, held.

4
Agni turns vishama

Erratic, unreliable fire.

5
Ama

Residue: heavy, foggy, stuck.

When the lever is applied at step two

1
Trigger

The same thing lands.

2
Slow, even breath

The lever, applied here.

3
Vata steadies

The mind loses its speed.

4
Agni steady

The fire burns cleanly.

5
Ojas

Clarity, vitality.

The top row is “How a Thought Becomes an Ulcer” re-read through the Ayurvedic lens. The bottom row is the same chain with one change at the second step. The tradition’s own image: just as bellows fan a fire, well-regulated Vata kindles the digestive Pitta.

One Breath in the Gap

Where RRRR meets the breath

The RRRR Protocol names the gap between trigger and reaction. In that gap, try one slow breath in and a longer one out, with no holding. You are not suppressing the reaction. You are slowing the bellows before the fire flares.

Gentle breathing only on this card: no breath retention, no forced techniques. For more, see the Pranayama section, and ask a clinician first if heart, lung or pregnancy concerns are in the picture.

Seven Tissues, One Fountain

How food becomes a body, one layer feeding the next

“The Agni Engine” ends in ojas, and “The Descent into Matter” ends in a body made of food. This card is the part in the middle. Classical Ayurveda says digested food first becomes a nutrient fluid, and from it the body builds seven tissues, the Dhatus+Sanskrit: that which holds or supports. The seven tissues of classical Ayurveda — Rasa, Rakta, Mamsa, Meda, Asthi, Majja, Shukra — each said to be built from the one before., in a fixed order. Each layer is said to be built from the one before it, so the chain is only as strong as its early steps.

Word-trap: Rasa also means taste, and sap, in other places. Here it names the first tissue, the nutrient fluid itself.

The Seven, In Order

Rasa to Shukra

1
Rasa · Plasma & lymph

The first nutrient fluid. Carries nourishment everywhere.

2
Rakta · Blood

Carries life through the body and nourishes it.

3
Mamsa · Muscle

Support and covering for the frame.

4
Meda · Fat

Lubricates and insulates.

5
Asthi · Bone

The structural framework.

6
Majja · Marrow & nerve

Fills the bones.

7
Shukra · Reproductive

Creates life. The last tissue in the chain, before ojas.

The functions shown are the commonly attributed ones. Only the order of nourishment, one tissue feeding the next, has been checked against a source.

Ojas sits at the end of the chain as the refined essence of all of them. That is the fuller version of “clean digestion leaves ojas.” The tradition’s reasoning is that a weak early step starves everything after it, and that long-standing digestive trouble is why deeper tissues are said to thin, dry or tire late.

Ojas is often compared with immunity. That is a loose bridge, not a match: ojas is a traditional idea of resilience, not a laboratory value.

Reflect: nourishment moves downstream one step at a time. Where in your week is the first step being rushed?

This is the tradition’s model of nourishment, not anatomy or physiology. Modern physiology does not describe tissues forming one from the last. Read it as a map of dependence: later layers rest on earlier ones.

Six Stages Before a Diagnosis

How an imbalance escalates, and where it is easiest to turn

“Two Kinds of Illness” asks where illness comes from. This card asks how it grows. Sushruta+Classical Indian physician, traditionally credited with the Sushruta Samhita, the foundational Ayurvedic text on surgery. The six-stage account of disease on this card comes from his tradition.’s tradition describes six stages, the Shat Kriya Kala+Sanskrit: the six stages of action or opportunity. The classical Ayurvedic account of how a disturbance progresses from quiet build-up to a settled disease, with each stage a chance to intervene., from a quiet build-up to a settled condition. Its quiet claim is that the first two stages are the cheapest to change.

The Six Stages

Sanchaya to Bheda

1
Sanchaya · Accumulation

A dosha builds in its home territory. Mild discomfort, and cravings for whatever feeds it.

2
Prakopa · Aggravation

It fills its container and begins to agitate. Restlessness, heat or heaviness with a direction.

3
Prasara · Overflow

It spills out of its home into general circulation.

4
Sthana Samshraya · Relocation

It lodges in a weak spot elsewhere in the body.

5
Vyakti · Manifestation

Symptoms declare themselves. The stage a chart can finally name.

6
Bheda · Diversification

Chronic, complex, deeply set.

Read this site’s way, the “Seven Signs of Load” sit at stages one and two: a coated tongue or a flat morning is not a condition; it is the build-up, and the cheapest moment to change what you take in and when. The model also echoes “The Body Keeps a Clock,” where illness is said to strike at the junctures between seasons; the tradition pairs the stages with the turning seasons too.

Reflect: which of the first two stages is quietly running in your week, and what are you still feeding it?

This is how the tradition reads a build-up, not a test and not a reason to wait. A symptom that worries you needs clinical care at any stage, and by the later stages the kitchen alone is not enough. The early stages are about noticing, not about delaying.

Channels, Not Nadis

Srotas — the roads things travel along

“The Agni Engine” says ama brings stagnation. Later tradition ties that stagnation to the body’s channels, though Charaka+Classical Indian physician, traditionally credited with the Charaka Samhita, the foundational Ayurvedic text on internal medicine. The channels (srotas) on this card are described there.’s own account of what disturbs them names food, habits, suppressed urges and emotion rather than ama. In Ayurveda these channels are the Srotas+Sanskrit: channels or streams. The body’s transit networks in Ayurveda — the roads along which food, breath, fluids, tissue and waste travel.: the roads along which food, breath, fluids, tissue and waste move. Not to be confused with the Nadis on the Hatha Yoga cards, which are a later and different use of the word: subtle energy channels, not the body’s transit roads.

Word-trap: Nadi carries three meanings. Charaka lists it among the synonyms for srotas. Hatha Yoga later uses it for the subtle energy channels (Ida, Pingala, Sushumna). And in Ayurvedic pulse reading, Nadi Pariksha, it means the pulse, a trained practitioner’s craft that this site does not teach and that is not a self-test.

Thirteen Roads

The classical list, in three families

Intake
Three roads

Pranavaha (breath), Annavaha (food), Udakavaha (water).

Tissue
Seven roads

One for each tissue in “Seven Tissues, One Fountain”: Rasavaha, Raktavaha, Mamsavaha, Medovaha, Asthivaha, Majjavaha, Shukravaha.

Waste
Three roads

Purishavaha (stool), Mutravaha (urine), Svedavaha (sweat).

Charaka calls these thirteen the important channels, not the whole count: every structure has its own, and a thoughtful reader is meant to infer the rest. He also describes a mind channel, Manovaha, in other passages, outside his list of thirteen. Sushruta’s count differs too: eleven pairs, with no bone, marrow or sweat channel, and a menstrual one (Artavavaha) added. Manovaha matches this site’s reading: the mind has its own road, said to be clogged mostly by Rajas and Tamas, the same two gunas as on “The Three Gunas,” and “How a Thought Becomes an Ulcer” is what happens when that road overloads.

Four Ways a Channel Fails

Classically, disease is a road going wrong

1
Sanga · Blockage

Flow is held up. It can be a true obstruction, pressure from outside the channel, or movement simply arrested with nothing solid in the way. Later tradition ties ama to this failure.

2
Atipravritti · Overflow

Too much flows, beyond the channel’s normal measure. The classical examples are loose stools, excess urine and excess acid.

3
Siragranthi · Knotting

Nodules or knots appear along the channel and hinder the flow. Modern reviews give the varicose vein as the usual example.

4
Vimarga-gamana · Wrong way

Contents leave their own channel and spill into another, or out of it. Two costs follow: irritation where they land, and starvation of the tissue they were meant to feed.

The examples come from modern reviews reading Charaka’s terse four-item list; the classical text itself gives little more than the names. Charaka’s own summary is shorter still: channels that are disturbed give rise to disease, channels that are cleared give ease.

What clogs the roads, in Charaka’s account, is the rule from “Like Increases Like” again: food and habits that share a dosha’s qualities and oppose the tissue’s own. His list is not only about food. Excess worry is named among what clogs the Rasa channel, and anger, grief and fear among what disturbs the sweat channel.

The practical echo of “Seven Signs of Load” is the same: if, as later tradition says, ama blocks the roads, take in less, and let one thing finish before the next arrives.

A traditional map of function, not anatomy. Several channels loosely track modern systems, breath with the respiratory and food with the digestive, but the match is loose and this site does not claim it.

The Fan Keeps Spinning

What knowing changes about the body — and what it does not

Traditional Source

Vedanta splits karma into what is dissolved by knowing and what is not. Knowing ends the identification that generates new binding action. But Prarabdha — the momentum of what already set this body in motion — must play out. The Panchadasi’s image is a fan: cut the current and it keeps turning on momentum alone.

The Cut
The Plug

Knowing removes the “electricity” — the belief that this body is the one who is ill, ageing, or owed a different outcome.

What Remains
The Momentum

The blades still turn. The body still ages, tires, hurts, and falls ill; the text never says otherwise.

The Posture
Audience, Not Actor

The sage experiences pain and pleasure like an audience at a magic show — seeing it happen, knowing it is a display.

Two practical readings for anyone working on their own health. Illness arriving after years of practice is not evidence of failing at it — the tradition expects the momentum to remain. And the Witness is not a treatment. The same lamp lights the stage whether the play is comedy or tragedy, and keeps shining when the hall empties in deep sleep; it does not rewrite the script.

This is a statement about the sage’s body in the text, not a diagnostic tool. It is not a way to read anyone’s illness as karma owed, and it does not replace treatment: take the medicine and also see who is taking it. Svasthya again — not the absence of disturbance, but staying established while the momentum runs.

Source: Panchadasi (Vidyaranya), via Swami Krishnananda, The Philosophy of the Panchadasi. Related on this page: The Two Illnesses.

The Kitchen Pharmacy

Treatment clears the way; then same herb, different preparation, and the questions before any remedy

Nature Does the Healing

Treatment clears the way; it does not supply the cure

The tradition states it bluntly: no physician has ever cured even the simplest disease. Read as hyperbole, the point is still about agency. A disease arises in time and carries its own ending. Treatment, on this view, removes obstacles and hastens a process that was already underway.

That fits Svasthya. If health is abiding in the Self, the practitioner’s job is to clear the way, not to supply a cure from outside. It also fits the line in “How a Thought Becomes an Ulcer”: medicine treats the ulcer, and rarely asks what was racing upstream.

This is the tradition’s philosophy, offered as a lens on agency, not as advice to wait out illness. Acute and serious illness needs clinical care.

Same Herb, Different Preparation

The extraction spectrum — heat, force, and burden

Classical Ayurvedic pharmaceutics, systematised in texts such as the Charaka Samhita and the Sharangdhara Samhita+A classical Ayurvedic compendium from roughly the 13th century (samhita means “collection”). One of the classical sources for the five basic preparation forms laid out below. (roughly the 13th century), treats how a plant is prepared as part of the medicine itself. One herb, five forms, laid along a single gradient:

The Five Forms

Swarasa, kalka, hima, phanta, kwatha

Swarasa
Fresh Juice

Pressed raw. The heaviest to digest.

Kalka
Paste

Crushed whole. High raw potency, still heavy.

Hima
Cold Infusion

Steeped overnight. Gentle; keeps the volatile.

Phanta
Hot Infusion

Brief steep in hot water. Moderate in force.

Kwatha
Decoction

Boiled down. Strongest extraction, lightest on digestion.

As heat rises, extraction force rises and digestive burden falls. Raw is not the same as gentle — and the strongest isn’t always the heaviest.

Read it as a lens on practice, not only on herbs: the same insight, taken raw or prepared, lands differently in the same person. Preparation is part of the teaching.

The Tamarind Case

When a recipe carries a reason nobody wrote down

Modern Research

“Same Herb, Different Preparation” says how a remedy is prepared is part of the remedy. This card adds a second lesson: a recipe can also encode its place. In parts of Andhra Pradesh the groundwater carries high natural fluoride, which over years can cause fluorosis, a damaging buildup in teeth and bone. Tamarind has long been cooked into the local pulses.

The telling goes that tamarind binds the fluoride in the water and keeps the body from absorbing it, so when villagers replaced it with the imported, “modern” tomato, they lost that protection and crippling fluorosis followed.

An Independent Check

One small trial on the tamarind half of the story

Setup
18 boys

Hostel boys in two Andhra districts, on a rice-and-pulse diet, first without and then with 10 g of tamarind a day.

Result
3.5 to 4.8

Fluoride excreted in urine, in mg per day, rose when tamarind was added.

The catch
Not free

Magnesium and zinc excretion fell too, and the mechanism is unclear. A change in urinary pH was the researchers’ guess.

The authors concluded tamarind is likely to help delay fluorosis. Note the difference from the telling above: they measured fluoride leaving in urine and did not show binding in the gut.

The trial supports the tamarind half only. The swap itself, tomato for tamarind and then whole villages falling ill, rests on a single account and has not been independently confirmed. Hold it as a well-told case, not a settled finding. Either way, the point stands: a traditional ingredient plausibly doing a job nobody had written down.

The lesson is not that old is better. It is that you do not remove a practice until you know what it was doing. The same caution applies to the practices on this site.

Reflect: which habit in your week would you drop first, and do you know what it is quietly holding up?

Not a treatment. Fluoride in drinking water is solved at the water source, and symptoms of fluorosis or any bone or dental concern belong with a clinician. One short trial in boys does not make tamarind a remedy.

Six Questions Before Any Remedy

Why there is no universal formula

The tradition won’t pick a preparation until six things are asked. Two people with the same complaint can leave with different answers — that is the design, not an inconsistency. Underneath all six runs one rule: Like Increases Like.

The Six Questions

Herb, dosha, agni, stage, medium, person — and the carrier

1
The Herb

Are its active principles volatile or stable? That decides cold steeping or boiling.

2
The Dosha+One of three biological energies in Ayurveda — Vata, Pitta, Kapha — patterns of function governing body and mind. Introduced in “The Three Doshas.”

Vata leans toward oils and warmth; Pitta toward cooling liquids; Kapha toward dry powders. “The Three Doshas” introduces them.

3
The Agni+Digestive fire — the capacity to transform what is taken in, whether food, medicine, or experience.

A weak digestive fire needs light preparations; a strong one can take heavy ones.

4
The Stage

Acute states call for fast, water-based forms; long-standing ones allow slow, building fats.

5
The Medium

Water-soluble and fat-soluble principles need different carriers.

6
The Person

Will they take it, and willingly? Palatability counts, because healing is partly psychological.

The Anupana+The carrier a remedy is taken with — honey, ghee, milk, warm water — chosen because it changes where the medicine acts. principle adds one more layer: the carrier steers the remedy — honey toward Kapha, ghee toward Pitta, sesame oil toward Vata. The vehicle changes the destination.

Sixth on the list, and rarely skipped by honest clinicians: a remedy you cannot bear to take is not yet medicine. The same goes for any practice on this site. If it only works when you force it, it needs re-preparing, not more willpower.

The Kitchen Shelf

Try it, notice, and keep what holds

Traditional Source

Every card before this one is vocabulary. This one is a shelf. These are everyday kitchen uses that were household practice long before the modern pharmacy, and they do not compete with it. They are for small, ordinary things, and each can be checked in your own body, which is the test a traditional claim has to pass: does it hold when practised?

Four Moments of the Day

Where the shelf meets an ordinary day

Morning
Wake-up

A quarter teaspoon of turmeric in a cup of warm water or milk, or the water from one teaspoon of fenugreek seeds soaked overnight in a glass of water, a cold infusion as in “The Five Forms.”Where you may notice it: the gut, and how heavy or light the morning feels.

With the meal
Cook, don’t capsule

Cumin, coriander, onion, garlic and ginger go into the pot at midday, when “The Body Keeps a Clock” says the fire is strongest. Half a raw onion bulb a day, sliced into the meal, is the traditional advice for the heart, for anyone comfortable eating raw onion.Where you may notice it: digestion at the meal itself, and the heart over the long run.

After the meal
A small chew

Half to one teaspoon of fennel seeds, or one cardamom pod, chewed slowly. A long-standing after-meal habit across India.Where you may notice it: the mouth at once, and the stomach as the meal settles.

Evening
Wind down

A cup of warm milk with a small pinch of nutmeg (no more than an eighth of a teaspoon) or one crushed cardamom pod. A pinch means a pinch.Where you may notice it: the mind, in how easily you settle for sleep.

When Something Bothers You

Small complaints, simple kitchen answers

Heavy stomach
Ginger

A thin, coin-sized slice of fresh ginger with a pinch of salt before eating, or a thumb-sized piece simmered in a cup of water and sipped slowly.Where you may notice it: the stomach, usually within the hour.

Scratchy throat
The warm drink

A thumb-sized piece of ginger, a quarter teaspoon of cinnamon and a pinch of pepper steeped in a cup of hot water; tulsi (holy basil) leaves can go in the same pot. Stir in a teaspoon of honey once it has cooled, as in “The Kitchen Rules.”Where you may notice it: the throat and chest, as warmth and soothing.

Stuffy nose
Ajwain

Crush about a teaspoon of ajwain+Carom seeds, also called bishop’s weed. A small, thyme-scented seed used across Indian kitchens. seeds in a clean cloth and breathe in slowly.Where you may notice it: the nose, within minutes.

Sore tooth
One clove

Hold a whole clove against the sore tooth until you can see a dentist. It numbs; it does not fix.Where you may notice it: the gum around the tooth, for a short while.

Two things change the result: the amount and the person. The amounts here are ordinary kitchen amounts for one adult, per day. Start at the low end. Heating, sharp things such as raw onion, ginger and pepper land differently in a hot, sharp constitution than in a heavy, slow one, which is why “The Six Questions” keep asking who is taking it. “The Three Doshas” is the place to start.

Try it and notice: pick one item, use it at the same time each day for a week, and write one line before and one after. If you cannot tell the difference, that is also an answer. Keep what holds and drop what doesn’t.

Where the shelf stops. Some of these interact with medicines (ginger and garlic with blood thinners, fenugreek and cinnamon with diabetes medication), and some are not for pregnancy or nursing. Anything severe, sudden, or lasting more than a few days, or arriving with fever, chest pain or bleeding, belongs with a clinician. This shelf sits beside medicine, not in place of it. If conventional care hasn’t helped with something everyday, it is a gentle thing to try alongside it, and your clinician should know about it.

The Kitchen Rules

Freshness, timing, and knowing your limits

Traditional kitchen guidance reduces to a few habits. They are stated here as the tradition states them; this site shares the logic and, on “The Kitchen Shelf,” ordinary kitchen amounts, not prescriptions.

The Five Rules

Fresh, heat, vessel, grain, limits

Fresh
Take It Fresh

Decoctions are meant to be made and used within hours. Re-warmed leftovers are said to leave Ama+Undigested residue — what is left when something was taken in but not fully processed..

Heat
Spare the Honey

Honey is added after cooling, never to something boiling hot.

Vessel
Let It Breathe

Decoctions are boiled in an open, wide vessel so evaporation does the concentrating.

Grain
Coarse, Not Dust

Coarse powders filter cleanly and resist charring; fine dust does not.

Limits
Consult First

Never replace prescribed medication with a home remedy without speaking to a physician.

The arc under all of these cards: raw nature, transformed by method, calibrated to one person, then assimilated by their own fire. Ayurveda’s aim isn’t to silence the symptom but to prepare what is raw into something this body can actually use. Svasthya, again: not the absence of disturbance, but the capacity to digest what arrives.

The Masters at a Glance

Six teachers. Two hemispheres. One destination.

The path of subtilization was never the property of one tradition. East and West independently arrived at the same map —By holding different lanterns. See the full coordinate-by-coordinate reference in the Master Matrix.

Tap a teacher to jump to their card

Section collapsed by default — tap to expand all six masters

The Eastern Lineage

Bhakti Yoga · ISKCON

Srila Prabhupada

Taught through a systematic methodology requiring authoritative intellect, and logical deduction — treating the science of the soul with the same rigor as any verifiable discipline, not as private feeling.

Metaphor: The physics of the soul. Knowledge as verifiable science.

The Art of Living

Gurudev Sri Sri Ravi Shankar

Taught through breath, silence, and present-moment awareness — moving practitioners from a localized, defended ego toward an experience of infinite, expanding consciousness.

Metaphor: The expanding space. Localized ego dissolving into the room it was always inside of.

Buddhism · The Middle Way

The Buddha

Taught through direct observation of suffering itself — not a revealed doctrine handed down, but a method anyone could verify by examining their own mind closely enough.

Metaphor: The raft. A teaching built to be used and then set down, not worshipped as the destination.

The Western Lineage

Classical Greek · The Examined Life

Socrates

Taught through relentless question, not doctrine — stripping away every inherited assumption until only what could survive scrutiny remained. The unexamined life, in his accounting, was not worth living.

Metaphor: The midwife. Drawing out a truth the student already carried, rather than installing a new one.

Stoicism · Roman Imperial Period

Marcus Aurelius

Taught through private discipline rather than public doctrine — an emperor writing nightly reminders to himself that status, applause, and even the empire were never the territory a person actually governs.

Metaphor: The citadel. An inner fortress no circumstance is permitted to breach. Marcus and Seneca, in depth, open below ↓

Contemporary · Present-Moment Teaching

Eckhart Tolle

Taught through the dissolution of psychological time — locating suffering not in circumstance itself, but in the mind's compulsive narration of past and future as the only moment that has ever existed.

Metaphor: The vertical dimension. Depth available in this instant, not a destination reached later.

Stoicism in Depth

Marcus Aurelius · The Citadel, Built

Handling difficult people: before, during and after

Marcus never wrote Meditations for readers. It is the private notebook of an emperor — years of frontier war, and in 175 AD a betrayal by his own general, Avidius Cassius, who declared himself emperor after a false report of Marcus’s death. What fills the pages is not statecraft. It is a tired man arguing with himself about how to treat the people who frustrate him.

Metaphor: The shield and the bridge. Protection first, so that cooperation never costs you yourself.

Traditional Source — Marcus Aurelius, Meditations (George Long translation, public domain).

01
Morning Armor
Prepare · Meditations 2.1

Marcus began the day by naming who he would meet: the busybody, the ungrateful, the arrogant, the deceitful, the envious, the unsocial. Most anger is surprise — you expected a fair hearing and got steamrolled, and now you stew all afternoon. Rehearsed in advance, rudeness arrives as ordinary instead of offensive. Seneca’s premeditatio malorum, below, aims this same armor at fortune; Marcus aims it at people.

02
Turn the Mirror
Prepare · Meditations 10.30

When someone’s fault offends you, turn to yourself at once and ask where you do the same. The coworker who keeps interrupting is the easy case: how often do you talk over people when you are excited? If a fault drives you up the wall, a spouse or close friend could probably name a few examples of you doing exactly that. Empathy begins with self-indictment — not as punishment, but as a way to take the heat out of the outrage.

03
The Faulty Math
Interpret · Meditations 7.63

Lying, taking credit, bullying a junior colleague: the Stoics, following Socrates and Plato, read these as errors of judgment, not malice. The person believes the behaviour buys status, power or security, and pays a cost they cannot see. The full reasoning sits with the four prepared responses in Forgiveness Without Becoming A Doormat.

04
The Inner Citadel
Defend · Meditations 5.2

Marcus wrote of how easy it is to wipe away every troublesome impression and be at once in tranquillity. Outside events cannot reach the mind without its permission. A hostile email at 4:55 on a Friday, a wasted Saturday, a missed promotion can wreck a schedule, but they cannot make you dishonest or petty unless you agree to take part. Close the laptop, let the sting wear off, respond on Monday. It is the same move as “Position as the Screen” in the STOP sequence.

05
Action Plus Story
Defend · Meditations 4.7

Their action plus your story equals perceived harm. A close friend forgets your birthday: that is the action. “They never cared” versus “they had a rough week and lost track of time” is the story, and you added it within seconds. The action belongs to them; the judgment is yours. This is the Separation Technique in Full Attention, pointed at a grievance.

06
Minimum Cooperation
Integrate · Meditations 2.1

We are made for cooperation, Marcus wrote — like feet, like hands, like eyelids, like the rows of the upper and lower teeth. Cooperation does not mean friendship; you do not have to grab a beer with a hostile person. It means firm, polite boundaries around a shared goal. With a neighbour who complains about everything, it can mean agreeing on the one fence repair you both care about and leaving the rest alone. The Ripple carries the same move into groups.

Read together, the first lessons are a shield and the last is a bridge. You cannot cooperate with difficult people while you are continually exposed to their chaos, so protection comes first and makes the cooperation possible.

“Take away thy opinion, and then there is taken away the complaint, ‘I have been harmed.’ Take away the complaint, ‘I have been harmed,’ and the harm is taken away.” — Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 4.7

Honest limit: reading harm as a story you add is a discipline for the sting of ordinary friction — a rude email, a forgotten birthday. It is not a claim that nothing real ever happens to you. Accountability, boundaries and walking away stay available, and where there is genuine abuse or danger the right move is protection, not reinterpretation.

Source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 2.1, 4.7, 5.2, 7.63, 10.30.

Seneca · The Three Pillars

Time, adversity and restlessness

Seneca taught the same discipline turned toward a different target: not the emperor's power but the ordinary day. His warning was that most people live as if life were a rehearsal for a better one that starts once conditions are right — and that the waiting never actually ends, because every arrival just reveals the next thing to wait for.

Metaphor: The rounded whole. A single day, lived and closed on its own terms, is a complete life — not a fragment of an unfinished one.

Traditional Source — Seneca, Letters from a Stoic, Letter I: “begin at once to live, and count each separate day as a separate life.”

That single-day discipline is the entry point into a fuller blueprint — three separate letters, one on time, one on adversity, one on restlessness, for how the citadel above is actually built. His starting move is a correction, not a complaint: the physician Hippocrates said life was short and art was long; Seneca's answer was that life isn't short, it's squandered — and a squandered abundance and a genuine shortage produce the exact same result, so they get treated as the same problem.

Pillar I
The Audit of Time

Reclaiming agency from distraction and “busy idleness” — motion mistaken for a life.

Pillar II
The Invulnerable Citadel

Stripping fear from adversity, poverty, and grief before they arrive, not after.

Pillar III
The Cure for Restlessness

Euthymia — a steady firmness of mind amid the endless tossing of unfulfilled desire.

Pillar I — the leaky vessel. It doesn't matter how much time is given if there's nowhere for it to settle; it escapes through the cracks of a distracted mind — social obligation, ambition, useless study, vain display — the same way water escapes a cracked jar no matter how much keeps getting poured in. Time is abundant. A mind full of ever-changing wants is what turns it into a sieve.

The PreoccupiedThe Wise
The PastFear it — ill-spent time becomes obvious in recollectionRevere it — sacred, untroubled, recalled at will
The PresentSquander it — short, stolen by distractionSeize it — organized as though it were the last
The FutureAnxious for it — defers living, hangs on tomorrowPrepares for it — matches time's speed with its own

Pillar II — wealth and grief, re-measured. Seneca's ledger for Apicius, a man of ten million sesterces and infinite desires, comes out net poverty — he poisoned himself believing that sum meant starvation. Diogenes, with zero assets and zero liabilities, comes out net wealthy. Nothing satisfies greed, but even a little satisfies nature — the mind sets the wealth, not the estate. Grief gets the same re-measuring, not elimination: feeling none is inhuman callousness, feeling endless sorrow is foolish self-indulgence — the aim is to feel the longing and still conquer it by reason, not to outrun it with travel or busyness, which only delay its return.

Premeditatio malorum — the armor of anticipation. Fortune falls heaviest on whoever it catches by surprise; rehearsing disease, disgrace, exile, and ruin in advance is what lets the first blow land without doing full damage.

Julius Canus, condemned to death by the tyrant Gaius, spent his final ten days playing draughts — asking only that the centurion confirm he was winning by one piece before the execution.

Pillar III — the cure for sea-sickness. Seneca diagnosed his friend Serenus with a mind that was neither well nor truly ill — tossing like an insomniac, loathing its own leisure, traveling endlessly only to discover itself as the most tedious companion on the trip. The prescribed cure was Euthymia: a smooth, steady course, well-disposed to itself, free of the ups and downs of circumstance — reached not by unbroken effort, which saps the mind until it snaps, but by deliberately alternating focus and release. Divide the day the way Asinius Pollio did, who read no letters past the tenth hour. Walk outdoors. Play, the way Socrates played with children and Scipio danced. Take wine occasionally to wash away care — short of habit, not as one.

All three pillars run the same operation: withdraw value from the outer ring — wealth, applause, tyrants, sickness, grief, none of it actually governable — and concentrate it entirely in the inner core: tranquility, purposeful action, the audit of time, virtue. “He will live badly who does not know how to die well.” Live as though lent to yourself, ready to return the loan on demand, with gratitude and good will.

“If you want to know how rich you are, try to find how many things you have that money cannot buy.”

— Radhanath Swami

Net worth was never the indicator. The true ledger counts what was acquired that no transaction could have purchased — the things still present after the money, the title, and the applause are gone.

Six different vocabularies. Six different centuries. The same person, arrived at from six different directions.

The Master Matrix of Existence

6 Material Stages × 7 Spiritual Layers = 42

Every possible human experience can be mapped to a specific coordinate in this grid. You are somewhere on it right now.

The body ages horizontally. Consciousness must ascend vertically. Most people move only left to right — never up.

Read the rows as a turn, not only a stack: layers 1–3 construct, layer 4 is the switch, layers 5–7 deconstruct. The highlighted cells (Shifting beliefs at 4, Trauma at 5, Crisis and Rigidity at 6) sit on that turn. The Path of Subtilization walks it.

A second, unrelated tally of what it takes to run this grid at all also lands on 42 — see The System Requirement.

Tap a row to jump to its full detail

“Your life purpose unfolds through the activities you engage in on the horizontal dimension — the dimension of doing. But everybody eventually finds that operating only on the horizontal dimension never satisfies them. There is another dimension — the vertical dimension, the dimension of being. The mastery of life is the dance between the two.”

— Eckhart Tolle

This table expands directly on The Ascent of Self and the Path of Subtilization — same seven layers, now with the full reference for each. For proof this map was never one tradition's alone, the Masters at a Glance shows six teachers across two hemispheres arriving at the same destination independently.

Each mode swaps the columns — nothing repeats. Tap a row’s + for Mastery, the one dimension with no column of its own.

Collapsed by default — tap to expand the reading guide

Read it two ways at once. Down the left, 7 layers — Body, Breath, Mind, Intellect, Memory, Ego, Self / Soul — run from the densest part of you to the subtlest, each one living out the exact same journey below in its own vocabulary. Across the top, that journey unfolds in 6 stages, and they aren’t arbitrary labels but five human sensory organs driving every one of them, at every layer, just wearing different clothes each time — tap the icon to see how:

Birth Silence+Not the absence of noise — the primal state where the ego's commentary dissolves and existence becomes something you can actually encounter. opens Space through 👂 Hearing+Sound needs physical space and air to travel — deep silence is what makes you suddenly feel the size of the room, or the emptiness, around you.
Growth Light+Not just illumination — the medium through which meaning is bestowed, carving comprehensible form out of raw chaos. brings Meaning through 👀 Sight+Vision is how humans gather most of their data — the eye turns raw light waves into recognizable shape and meaning almost instantly.
Sustenance Chaos+Not disorder to be defeated — the field of pure potentiality every genuine act of creation actually comes from. supplies Energy through 👅 Taste+Taste is a chemical gatekeeper screening fuel for the body — eating breaks molecular chaos down into a direct burst of physical energy.
Transformation Beauty+Not an ornament — a mode of cognition, a way of knowing reality that concept and reason alone can't reach. offers Cognition through 👃 Smell+Smell bypasses logic and goes straight to the brain's emotion and memory centers — an ancient, instant form of cognition, judging beauty or warning before you've thought at all.
Deterioration & Death Art+Not a finished product — the ongoing relationship through which a person participates in existence, bridging self and world. establishes Connection through ✋ Touch+The most intimate sense, requiring physical proximity — shaping material into art bridges the internal self with the external world.

Reading further right: Brainwave+The measurable state your brain is actually in at this layer., Awareness+What that brainwave state feels like from inside, in the moment you're living it., and Stage+The inner work that particular combination is asking of you right now. read as one arc, not three separate facts. Alchemy+The corresponding stage in the old alchemical Great Work — base matter refined, step by step, toward gold. and Existence Layer+The matching Sanskrit kosha, or sheath, from the older Vedantic map of the self. are correspondence — older maps drawing the same line in a different language.

One more correspondence, underneath the Existence Layer column: Yogic philosophy nests these same seven koshas inside three coarser bodies (Sariras+Sanskrit for “bodies” — the physical, subtle, and causal vehicles said to house the five koshas, coarsest to subtlest.) — the same three bodies laid out in full in Neti Neti’s Three Bodies. Annamaya alone makes up the Gross Body (Sthula Sarira). Pranamaya, Manomaya, and Vijnanamaya together make up the Subtle Body (Sukshma Sarira) — the bridge layers, Layers 2 through 4 below. Anandamaya alone makes up the Causal Body (Karana Sarira), said to be the one that survives the body's death. Same seven layers. One more way to group them.

The Transcendence Paradox — Why Layer 7 Is Different

Layers 1 through 6

Bound by time. They experience Birth, Growth, Sustenance, Transformation, Deterioration, and Death on repeat — the wheel of Samsara+The cycle of birth, death, and rebirth — the ceaseless churn of conditioned existence every layer below the Self remains bound to.. No escape from the horizontal pull of matter.

Layer 7 — The Self / Soul

Outside of time. It does not deteriorate. While the Ego experiences Dissolution, the Soul simply Transcends and remains Unchanged. It steps off the grid of mortality entirely.

Why do 7 spiritual layers share only 6 stages of material realization? Because the 7th layer breaks the rules of matter.

Layers 1 through 6 are one and the same bondage — the wheel of Samsara traced at The Root Diagnosis (and, in the Shiva Sutras’ own terms, The Bondage of “Knowing”). Layer 7 is the only way out.

The Only Question That Remains

The horizontal movement is already happening — without your permission.

The vertical movement takes one decision: you are more than the layer you currently inhabit. Not a destiny — an invitation.

A Closer Look — Memory

You’re not living your past. You’re living memory’s latest cut of it.

A closer look at Layer 5 — Memory in the Master Matrix, for anyone who wants to sit with this layer a while longer than a table row allows.

Tap to expand — how memory selects, weighs, links & narrates, plus habit vs. pure memory and the cone of memory

What Layer 5 Actually Keeps

Plus the same event, remembered into two different selves.

Layer 5 does not keep your life exactly as it happened. It keeps the version memory hands back.

Each time a memory returns, something is adjusted. A detail is sharpened. Another is softened. A meaning is added later.

What shapes identity is often not the moment itself, but the version that stayed.

The Same Event, Two Different Selves

This is why two people can live through the same event and carry different selves afterward. The moment was shared. The inner version was not.

Much of what you call “me” was built this way — not only in the moment, but afterward, as memory kept sorting, weighing, and retelling.

Four Things Chitta+The mind-stuff, or memory-store — the layer that holds impressions, conditioning, and habitual patterns built up over time. Is Doing Right Now

Selecting, weighing, linking, narrating — the four quiet jobs memory never stops doing.

Selecting

Not everything is kept. Memory decides what stands out and what fades.

Weighing

Some moments are made heavier than others. Pain, love, shame, pride — memory gives them different weight.

Linking

Memory connects one moment to another, building a larger story from scattered pieces.

Narrating

After enough retelling, the story starts to sound like simple fact: “This is just who I am.”

Two Ways To Relate To It

Getting ruled by the first version that settled, versus looking carefully enough to find what carries it.

Never Looks

Gets ruled by whatever version settled first, often under stress.

Looks Carefully

Honestly, without rushing to defend the story — and finds something deeper than memory itself: the one who carries it, the one who interprets it, the one who was never identical to it.

Two Kinds of Remembering

Habit-memory that acts versus pure memory that dreams — and the Bergson footnote worth noticing without signing up for.

Look closely, and “memory” is not one thing wearing two hats. It is two different activities that happen to share a name.

Habit-Memory

Memory that acts. Built by repetition, not recall. It doesn’t remember learning to ride a bike — it just rides.

It lives entirely in the present tense. No date attached. No story attached. Just the motion, ready to fire.

Pure Memory

Memory that dreams. Recorded once, whole, the moment it happened. Not the skill of riding — the specific afternoon, the specific fall, the specific scrape.

It has a date. It has a place. It surfaces on its own schedule, not yours.

The philosopher Henri Bergson pushed this further than most — he argued the two run on entirely separate tracks: habit-memory belongs to the body, pure memory belongs to the mind, and the brain’s only job is routing one into the other, not storing either. That’s a stronger claim than the site is making here. What’s worth noticing without signing up for the full theory: your two kinds of remembering really do behave differently — one is a reflex, the other is a visitor.

The Cone of Memory

Bergson’s shape for how the whole preserved past narrows down to the single point where you act.

The Shape of Remembering

Bergson also gave this relationship a shape — and the shape carries one of his stronger claims along with it: that the whole of your past is preserved somewhere, intact and indestructible, whether or not you ever revisit it. That’s a metaphysical bet, not an established fact — neuroscience doesn’t require a warehouse of untouched memories sitting in reserve. What’s worth keeping regardless of the bet is the shape itself: a genuinely useful way to picture the relationship between remembering and acting.

At the wide end, the whole past sits at rest — every version of you that has ever existed, still on file, unmoving, unconscious.

At the narrow end is a single point where that vastness touches down: the body, standing in the one moment that is actually happening.

Remembering is not opening a drawer. It is the whole cone narrowing until it fits through a single point.

How a Memory Becomes an Action

1. A Demand Arrives

Something in the present calls for a response. The body, at the point, has to act.

2. The Cone Narrows

Out of everything on file, only what’s relevant gets drawn down toward the point.

3. It Becomes Motion

At the apex, the memory stops being a memory and becomes whatever you just did.

Most of the time you only ever meet the point — the acting, present-tense sliver. The rest of the cone is still there, whether you go looking or not.

Memory is not the self. It is material.

Look closely enough, and the past stops being a prison. It becomes something you can finally understand.

None of these make you a bad person. They make you a person currently being run by the firewall instead of standing behind it. Spotting ego in a motive is not the same as seeing nothing but ego — some of what you do is simply good. The nine questions below go deeper into exactly where.

A Few Old Doors

Small stories, kept short on purpose.

No single tradition owns these. Read one, sit with it, move on — nothing here needs to be solved.

Tap to expand — twelve short parables from Zen, Sufi, Advaita, Taoist, Greek, Upanishadic, and modern sources

Zen

The Bucket and the Firewood

Asked what his practice was, a monk answered: when I chop wood, the wood is being chopped. When I carry water, the water is being carried. There's no one left over to be doing it.

Zen

I Cannot Say

At a funeral, a student asked his teacher: is the body in the coffin dead, or alive? “I cannot say,” the teacher answered — and took a beating rather than give a cleaner answer he didn't actually have.

Taoist · Liezi

The Archer Who Forgot the Bow

Sent to master archery, a student returned having forgotten what a bow even looked like. He could still bring down a bird with a glance. Some skills complete themselves by disappearing.

Greek

The Kingdom of Right Here

Alexander the Great, mid-conquest, found Diogenes resting in the sun and promised to relax once the world was his. Diogenes pointed out he was already relaxing, and had conquered nothing to get there.

Sufi

The Door Was Never Locked

Junnaid prayed for years for God to open the doors. The mystic Rabiya struck him and said: the doors are open. They always were. Get up and walk through.

Modern

The Portrait Is Not the Man

A woman once kissed a painted portrait of Van Gogh and praised its beauty. “Did the portrait answer you?” he asked. “No? Then it wasn't me.” A likeness is not the thing it resembles — including the words used to describe it.

Advaita

The Tenth Man

Ten friends cross a river. Once ashore, one counts to be sure everyone made it — and finds only nine, forgetting to count himself. All ten weep for the lost tenth, until a passerby points at the counter and says: you are the tenth. Nothing was ever missing. He just left himself out of his own count.

Advaita

The Untouchable Who Taught the Teacher

Returning from the Ganges, Shankaracharya asked a man in his path to step aside. The man asked which should move — the body, which is only matter, or the awareness inside it, which has no caste at all. The teacher had come home already knowing the answer. He'd just forgotten to live it for a moment.

Upanishadic · Mundaka

The Two Birds

Two birds perch on one tree, inseparable friends. One eats the tree's fruit — sweet, bitter, all of it. The other simply watches, eating nothing, untouched by any of it. The eating bird spends its whole life chasing the next fruit. The moment it finally looks up and recognizes the still one beside it as its own truer self, the hunger stops mattering.

Sufi

The Beggar and the Greater Beggar

Praying beside a Sufi fakir for glory and a lasting kingdom, King Akbar noticed the fakir simply get up and walk away. Asked why, the fakir said: why should a beggar go begging from an even greater beggar?

Zen

What He Was Still Carrying

Forbidden to touch women, a Guru waded in anyway, carried a drowning girl to the far bank, set her down, and walked on in total peace. His disciple touched nothing — and carried her, plus his outrage at the broken rule, in his head for three hours afterward. Only one of them was actually done with it.

Modern

Thirty Years on the Island

A wealthy man lived thirty years on a paradise island before a visiting journalist asked what it was like to live somewhere so beautiful. Only hearing it named out loud, he actually looked. He'd been standing in it the entire time.

Common Questions

The questions people ask when they start noticing.

The Default OS is the autopilot running underneath every decision, reaction and trade — the sum of your conditioning, firing as stimulus-response loops before you consciously choose. In Sanskrit: Vritti, the constant stream of mental chatter. It is not the enemy. It is the starting point: once you see the programme running, you can respond rather than react. That gap is where the RRRR Protocol lives. See The Framework →

The RRRR Protocol has two versions depending on what you are facing. Both start with the same first step — Recognize. That moment of noticing is where everything changes.

Version 1 — Stop the Impulse

Recognize → Resist → Return → Release

Use this when you need to stop impulsive behaviour before it happens — revenge trading, sending the angry message, reaching for the drink, reacting before you think. Recognize the trigger. Resist acting on the first impulse. Return to baseline (breathe, step away). Release the charge without acting on it. The behaviour never happens. This is the emergency protocol.

Version 2 — Process the Emotion

Recognize → Reflect → Reframe → Respond

Use this for emotional intelligence and deeper processing — navigating a difficult relationship, a career decision, grief, or a long-held pattern. Stopping the impulse isn’t enough here. You need to understand it. Recognize what triggered you. Reflect on what it is really activating underneath. Reframe the narrative — what is actually true? Then Respond from awareness, not reflex.

The 3-Step Circuit Breaker is the emergency interrupt for the autopilot. When the RRRR Protocol feels too structured for a moment of acute distress, this severs the automatic programme instantly.

The 3 Steps

1. Pause — Box Breathing

Inhale 4 seconds. Hold 4 seconds. Exhale 4 seconds. Hold 4 seconds. One complete box. This severs the neurochemical loop of the auto-pilot programme — no willpower required, just the breath.

2. Witness and Label

Step back. Ask: “What is the exact trigger causing this distress?” Naming the emotion strips its hidden power. You move from being inside the reaction to observing it from the screen.

3. Detached Action

Shift focus to what you can control. Act while remaining detached from the outcome — success or failure. Stop watering the weeds. Act from the SELF, not from the wound.

Use the Circuit Breaker for acute moments. Use the full RRRR Protocol for deeper processing and reflection.

Traditional Source — the Sallatha Sutta, Pali Canon.

The First Arrow is the pain itself — the loss, the diagnosis, the rejection, the loss on the chart. It lands whether you're ready or not, and no amount of awareness stops it from hitting.

The Second Arrow is the one you fire yourself, into the same wound: the story layered on top — this shouldn't be happening, this means I'm broken, this will never get better. The Buddha's teaching was blunt about the arithmetic — an untrained person struck by loss feels two arrows' worth of pain for one arrow's worth of event. The second one is optional. Almost no one declines it by default.

This is a different mechanism than RRRR or the Circuit Breaker. Those interrupt a reaction before it fires. The Second Arrow shows up after impact — it's not about stopping an impulse, it's about noticing the exact moment raw pain gets a narrative bolted onto it, and choosing not to pull the bow a second time. The pain was never optional. The suffering, most of it, was.

The Enneagram here is not a type to identify with. It is a map of who you are not — nine masks the ego uses to manage desire, fear and anger. Using it to justify behaviour (“I’m a Six, that’s why I act this way”) goes deeper into the trance; using it to see the fixation is the way out. Nine sides, one funnel — every fixation ends at the same void. See The Enneagram →

The Rasas are the nine intrinsic human emotions from the Ancient Vedic traditions. They define the body chemistry and emotional weather each ego type generates.

Each Enneagram type’s core belief creates a specific internal environment — and that environment naturally generates the body chemistry of one of the Nine Rasas. The Shadow Rasa is the distorted version. The Light Rasa is the Essence underneath.

The nine Rasas: Shringara (Love/Attachment), Hasya (Joy/Laughter), Karuna (Sadness/Compassion), Raudra (Anger/Rage), Vira (Courage), Bhayanaka (Fear/Terror), Vibhatsya (Disgust/Aversion), Adbhuta (Wonder/Marvel), Shanti (Peace/Serenity). See The Rosetta Stone of the Ego →
