The Buddha once gathered a few leaves in his hand and asked his monks: are there more leaves here, or in the forest? In the forest, they said. He replied that what he knew was like the forest — but what he taught was only the leaves in his hand. Not because the rest wasn’t true. Because a person facing an emergency doesn’t need the whole forest — only what's basic to living and curing the suffering in front of them. This site works the same way: a handful of leaves, picked for what's usable right now, not a claim to hold the whole forest.

Western psychotherapy and Eastern wisdom are not opposites — they are complements. The West gives the map: vocabulary for your suffering and cognitive insight. The East gives the resilience: holding suffering with spaciousness. Alan Watts said it best: look deeply into Buddhism, Taoism, Vedanta and Yoga and you find something resembling psychotherapy. See The Integration Engine →

No — it’s every tradition. Vedic philosophy calls it Moksha+Liberation — release from the cycle of rebirth and from mistaken identity with the small self.. Western mysticism calls it Divinization. Ancient Greeks called it Know Thyself. Modern psychology calls it Self-Transcendence. Every wisdom tradition in human history has arrived at the same conclusion: the highest achievement is looking inward to realize your true nature beneath the illusions of the ego. *SELF is not picking a tradition. It’s pointing at what they all found.
The one aim every other aim is pursued for the sake of: knowing your SELF. Career, family, and ambition remain valid sub-goals, as long as they never conflict with it or replace it. Read the full section →
Depends on what you believe. But here’s what’s certain: every deed, every reaction, every moment you spend in awareness or autopilot builds a balance sheet inside you. Whether that’s literal reincarnation, Karma+The law of cause and effect applied to action and intention — every deed, thought, and reaction leaves an imprint (Samskara) that shapes what comes next., or just the neurology of habit formation — the math is the same. You are becoming what you practice. See The Cosmic Ledger →

Because abstract ideas are hard to carry across thousands of years, and stories are not. A principle like “act without clinging to the result” is easy to nod at and easy to forget. Give it a charioteer, a battlefield, and a hesitating archer, and it survives retelling by people who never read a word of philosophy.

Image, song, festival, and daily ritual do the same job from other angles. They put the idea into the body and the calendar, so it gets practiced rather than merely believed. That is how a teaching reaches a farmer and a scholar in the same village.

You do not have to take any god literally for this to hold. Read the story as a carrier, and ask what it is carrying.

Whether a particular figure also encodes some scientific fact is a separate claim. *SELF does not rest anything on it.

The Vedic tradition describes four Ashramas+A stage of life — one of four phases (student, householder, forest-dweller, renunciate), each with its own duties and its own kind of freedom., each with a different main task:

1 · Brahmacharya
Student
Learn, build discipline, and form the character everything else will rest on.
2 · Grihastha
Householder
Work, family, and service. Where Karm Yog is practiced most directly: full obligations, held without clinging.
3 · Vanaprastha
Forest-dweller
Loosen the grip on roles and possessions. Pass duties on, and turn attention inward.
4 · Sannyasa
Renunciate
Release identification with roles altogether, and live from what remains.

It is a map, not a mandate. The useful question is which stage’s task you are actually avoiding.

Self-realization is not a destination you arrive at in one lifetime. That’s the feature, not the bug. The question isn’t “Am I there yet?” It’s “Am I pointed right?” Are you noticing more? Are you reacting less? Are you choosing from awareness instead of fear? If yes — you’re walking the path.

42 is a symbol, not a prediction. TO BE, SELF and JIVA each sum to 42 by alphanumerical value, and 42 is the ASCII code for the asterisk (*) — the wildcard that means “anything.” Douglas Adams meant it as a joke; we took it seriously enough to build a symbol on it. See Why 42 Is Not a Coincidence →

Two separate deadlines, not one. In roughly 1 to 1.5 billion years the brightening Sun tips Earth into a runaway greenhouse — the oceans evaporate and complex life can no longer survive. About 3.5 billion years later the Sun exhausts its core hydrogen and swells into a Red Giant, swallowing Mercury and Venus and engulfing or scorching Earth. See Why 42 Is Not a Coincidence →

That one thing only you can offer the world. Not necessarily a new innovation or technology — something the world needs that carries your unique mark. Ask yourself: “What would I be willing to pay for if I were on the other side of the value exchange?” If that is something only you can offer, that drives you, that you’re passionate about achieving — that is your worth. Not in dollars. In purpose. That discovery requires listening to your inner voice. No one else can do it for you.

What you can offer the world is set by the consciousness it comes from. A mind still reacting out of fear, ego and conditioning repeats itself, however good the intent — the contribution is capped by the awareness behind it. See The Ceiling of Contribution →

This is why the work is not optional decoration on top of a productive life — it is the precondition for one. Raising consciousness is not self-improvement for its own sake. It is what allows the value you bring — your work, your relationships, your decisions — to come from clarity instead of conditioning. Progress toward discovering SELF is, in this sense, the most practical thing a person can do: it raises the ceiling on everything else they touch.

The belief that “I am not enough” is an illusion — one that prevents us from seeing the truth that is already present.

Self-worth is not something to be earned or proven. It is simply a Realization — a recognition of who you truly are. A knowing.

I am the whole. The totality. That includes every part of me.

When we recognize our self-worth, that is when we step into our greatness. That is when we align with our authentic power. That is when we can finally realize our full, true potential.

I am worthy — and so are you.
The only question remaining: do you know it?

The four operational rules for daily life drawn from the *SELF framework. Simple enough to remember in the heat of a moment. Deep enough to govern a lifetime.

Rule 1

Comparison Culture — Compare only to your Yesterday’s self

Do not compare yourself to others. Only compare the person you were yesterday to the person you are today. Learn from mistakes. Figure out what works. Be the best version of yourself by adapting to your own circumstances.

Rule 2

The Starting Point — Begin exactly from where you stand

Begin exactly from where you are right now. Focus only on how you respond to life’s challenges — that is the only thing you control. Contain your energy. Direct it toward higher purpose instead of dissipating it through emotion.

Rule 3

The Direction — Be the change you want to see

If you do not dictate your own direction, you will be pulled into someone else’s. Practice mindfulness to return to the present moment — life is happening only right now, not in the past or future.

Rule 4

The Reality Check — Verify your goals against reality

Find people who have already achieved the goals you are pursuing. Ask: does the reality of that achievement align with your true inner needs? If not, reprogram the path. Start working on your inner SELF right now, so you will not regret it on your deathbed.

Viktor Frankl’s Logotherapy gives us three practical tools for discovering meaning beyond the symptom. These complement the RRRR Protocol by operating at a deeper level of questioning.

Dereflection — Shift to higher purpose

Shift focus from the problem to a higher purpose. Ask: What would your life look like without this problem? This moves attention from the wound to the direction.

Paradoxical Intention — Face the fear directly

Remove the power of fear by intentionally focusing on what you fear most. The anxiety about the anxiety is often worse than the thing itself. Name it fully and watch its grip loosen.

Socratic Dialogue — The answers are within

The answers do not come from outside. They are realized through careful questioning. Ask: Is there anything in your life you would die for? If yes — that is your direction towards the super-ordinate goal.

Forty-seven pages, five phases, built around real exercises rather than passive reading — the same spirit as the Feedback Loop above, just with room to actually write your answers down. Comes as a digital PDF in both dark and light theme.

Phase 1 — Where Are You Now

Catching the Default OS — the autopilot — running in real time, in your own life, not just in theory.

Phase 2 — The Inner Turn

The Arrival Fallacy, and turning attention inward instead of toward the next milestone.

Phase 3 — The Diverse Paths

Self-enquiry through three of five pillars — Who Am I, Where Am I From, What Can I Do — the longest phase, by design.

Phase 4 — Savoring the Footsteps

Walking through difficulty on purpose — RRRR, the 3-Step Circuit Breaker, and tools for the days the framework gets tested.

Phase 5 — The Final Destination

The remaining two pillars — Why Am I Here, Where Am I Going — plus a daily and weekly check-in loop to carry past the last page.

It exists because reading about a framework and sitting with your own answers to it are two different things. This site points at the map. The workbook is where you stop reading it and start walking it, one honest page at a time — with a baseline self-rating on page one you revisit after Phase 5, so the shift is something you can actually see in your own handwriting, not just something you're told happened.

It doesn’t hand you answers — *SELF doesn’t work that way. It hands you better questions, in an order designed to build on each other, phase by phase. And it says so plainly: finishing it won’t make you a finished, fully realized person. Nobody finishes this kind of work in one lifetime — that’s the actual shape of it, not a flaw.

Not a clinical depression to be treated — an initiation, the threshold experience every wisdom tradition has mapped. The common mistake is treating it as a malfunction: medicating the signal, waiting it out, reaching for the next distraction. The signal returns, louder. It does not end. It graduates. Read The Dark Night →

The sequence through which all experience reaches you: Object (the world) → Senses (your lenses) → Mind (the projector) → Consciousness (the Screen). Most people identify with the mind — the projector. Realization is recognising you are the Screen, not the film. See Before the Ego, the Field →

Sat-Chit-Ananda is the Sanskrit description of the true nature of the SELF — three inseparable qualities of what you actually are beneath the ego:

Sat — Existence / Being

You exist. This cannot be negated — even the thought “I do not exist” requires an exister. Sat is the bedrock. Unborn, undying, always-already present.

Chit — Consciousness / Awareness

You are aware. Right now, reading this, there is knowing. That knowing is not the brain — the brain is an object known by awareness. Chit is the light by which all experience is seen.

Ananda — Bliss / Joy

The natural resting state of pure awareness is contentless peace — a bliss that requires no trigger. This is not an emotion. It is what remains when grasping and aversion fall away.

Traditional Source — Why bliss, specifically? Sri Aurobindo's The Life Divine argues it can't be otherwise: consciousness existing within being is what makes self-awareness possible at all, and awareness aware of its own action is what delight is. Ananda isn't a fourth thing added to Sat and Chit. It's what Sat and Chit are, looked at from the side of feeling rather than the side of fact.

Self-Realization is not adding Sat-Chit-Ananda to who you are. It is recognizing that this is what you have always already been.

The Default OS is wired for novelty and threat, so anything constant — air, light, water — fades into background noise. That is habituation: efficient for survival, costly for gratitude. Before you drink water — pause. Before you breathe — notice. Gratitude is not sentiment — it is a recalibration. The full argument is in The Internal Public Offering →

We enter this world with zero self-made net worth. We leave with X. Nothing travels with us. Nothing, except how many hearts we touched.

True legacy is not net worth at peak. It is not the portfolio. It is not the name on a building or the followers on a chart. It is the number of hearts you touched with your genuine contribution — the imprint your SELF left on others that continues radiating after you leave.

Your SELF is the super-ordinate goal. The only one that cannot be taken, liquidated, or diluted. The only balance sheet that survives the final settlement.

Question is only whether you start realizing your true SELF before the deathbed?.

Reference

Glossary

This site borrows words from a few different traditions — Sanskrit psychology, alchemy, Hermetic philosophy, neuroscience. None of them are assumed knowledge. Look anything up here, or tap the + next to a word wherever you find it.

A Warning About This Glossary

The tradition's own caution against mistaking vocabulary for the thing it points at

One caution the tradition itself is blunt about: none of this is the thing it names. Being able to define Avarana+Sanskrit for “covering” or “veiling” — Maya's concealing power, one of its two inseparable functions alongside Vikshepa. or recite the four qualifications is skill with words, not the seeing those words point toward — a man who can only describe a rope isn't thereby free of the snake he still sees on the floor. Use the glossary to stop tripping over the vocabulary. Don't mistake fluency in it for having arrived.

Vivekachudamani+“Crest-Jewel of Discrimination” — a foundational Advaita Vedanta text attributed to Adi Shankaracharya, on the qualifications and inner work that lead to direct Self-knowledge. Names This Trap Directly

✕
The Dense Forest of Words

Loud speech, skill in expounding scripture, real erudition — all of it brings the scholar a measure of personal enjoyment, and causes the mind to ramble further. Useless for liberation, however impressive it sounds from the outside.

✓
The Direct Path

Direct knowledge of Brahman — the thing itself, seen, not merely described with increasing precision.

Without actually defeating one's enemies, no one gets to claim the throne just by repeating “I am the emperor.” A man already bitten by the snake of Ignorance is not saved by getting better at the terminology for snakebite.

The tradition actually splits knowledge into two kinds rather than dismissing the lower one outright. Apara Vidya+Worldly knowledge — grammar, science, scripture-as-information. Genuinely useful, and entirely powerless against suffering at the root. — grammar, chemistry, even scripture read as information — clears superficial ignorance of objects and is worth having. It simply can't reach the deeper ignorance it was never built to touch. Only Para Vidya+Supreme knowledge — direct self-knowledge, the only kind of knowing that reaches root ignorance rather than merely describing it. — direct self-knowledge — does that. This glossary, at its very best, is Apara Vidya. Useful for not tripping over words. Not a substitute for the other kind.

Isha Upanishad · 9–11

Both Together

Action alone
Darkness

Mere doing, mere pursuit of the material. It runs, and it runs blind.

Words alone
Greater Darkness

Mere verbal knowledge: learning the words and acting against them.

Held together
Across, and Beyond

One carries you across death. The other reaches immortality.

The passage above leans one way: words are not the seeing. This is the other half. The seeing doesn’t excuse you from the competence that keeps the chariot on the road. Someone has to hold the reins while the rider watches.

Honest limitThis is one reading. Modern commentary often glosses avidya as material science and vidya as spiritual knowledge. Shankara reads avidya as ritual action and vidya as meditative worship of a deity. Take the verses as a pointer, not a ruling.

Which of the two have you been leaning on?

Full Glossary

Every term this site borrows, defined in one place

Sanskrit & Yogic Psychology
TermDefinition
Atman The individual self, in Advaita Vedanta — but held as identical to, not separate from, universal consciousness. Not "a soul" in the sense of a separate possession; closer to the awareness doing the possessing.
Brahman The ground of all reality in Vedanta — not a deity to petition, but the substrate everything, including you, is made of and never actually separate from.
Prajnanam Brahma “Consciousness is Brahman” — one of the four Mahavakyas, from the Aitareya Upanishad. Points at what reality is made of.
Ayam Atma Brahma “This Self is Brahman” — one of the four Mahavakyas, from the Mandukya Upanishad. The sentence as direct experience reports it.
Nada Sanskrit for “sound.” In Nada Yoga, the inner sound attention can follow from coarse to subtle until only the listening remains.
Jiva The individual, experiencing self — distinct from Atman only in that Jiva is Atman as it appears bound to one particular body and story. Same light, wearing a name. Its letters also sum to 42 — see The Architecture of ‘TO BE’.
Kutastha “Standing like an anvil” — the unchanging baseline of consciousness that stays unaffected while the experiences of life beat on it. What gives every state the quality of “I am.”
Paroksha Indirect, mediated knowledge — through words, inference, or another’s report. Valid, and still one step removed from the thing known.
Aparoksha Immediate knowledge — no gap between knower and known. The kind Advaita says self-knowledge must be, which is why hearing alone is only the first half.
Upasana Sustained meditation on a chosen object — “sitting near.” In the Panchadasi, the bridge between indirect knowledge and direct realisation. Saguna (with attributes) or Nirguna (without).
Pratika A symbol held as a support for meditation — an image, a sound, or the whole universe taken as one vehicle. It does not have to be a deity.
Krama-mukti Liberation by degrees — the result the tradition assigns to Saguna Upasana, where the mind is purified progressively.
Sadyo-mukti Immediate liberation — the result the tradition assigns to Nirguna Upasana and direct inquiry, where the knower–known divide is dissolved at once.
Aviveka Non-discrimination — losing the ability to tell the real from the unreal. In the Panchadasi’s sequence it follows Avidya and precedes the ego-sense, so confusion comes before identification.
Prarabdha The momentum of past action that has already begun to bear fruit and set this body going. Knowing does not stop it; like a fan after the power is cut, it runs down on its own.
Tripti Supreme satisfaction — the last stage of the Tenth Man parable, where nothing is left to be obtained because nothing was ever missing.
Maya Usually translated "illusion," though "the measuring-out" is closer — the way one undivided reality appears to us as separate things, separate selves, and passing time.
Avarana Sanskrit for "covering" or "veiling" — Maya's concealing power, one of its two inseparable functions alongside Vikshepa. Hides the ground itself; doesn't distort it.
Vikshepa Sanskrit for "projection" or "scattering" — Maya's projecting power, which supplies an alternative the instant Avarana has cleared the space for one.
Mahamaya Literally "the great Maya" — the Shakta tradition's name for Maya worshipped as the Divine Mother's living power, rather than approached as ignorance to be dissolved.
Bahirmukha Sanskrit for "outward-facing" — the "I"-thought running from the Heart through the brain and sense organs to land on gross names and forms. The mind goes out, the world appears, the Self is obscured.
Antarmukha Sanskrit for "inward-facing" — the "I"-thought restrained at the Heart instead of chased outward. Names and forms disappear, the mind ends, and the Self remains as the residue.
Manonasa The permanent destruction of the mind at its root, achieved by Self-Enquiry — as distinct from Manonigraha, the mind's temporary suppression.
Manonigraha The temporary stilling of the mind through auxiliary aids — breath-control, mantra, form meditation — as distinct from Manonasa. Once the aid stops, residual impressions send the mind wandering again.
Cidākāśa Sanskrit for "the space of consciousness" — awareness described in the Ashtavakra Gita as a clear, unbounded space rather than a state to attain or a thought to think.
Chitta The mind-stuff, or memory-store — the layer that holds impressions, conditioning, and habitual patterns built up over time. Not thought itself, but the substrate thought leaves marks on.
Antahkarana Literally "the inner instrument" — the collective term in Vedanta for mind, intellect, memory-store, and ego-sense together: the machinery through which consciousness processes experience.
Ahamkara Literally "the I-maker" — the function of mind that takes raw experience and stamps "me" onto it, manufacturing a sense of separate identity out of what's actually happening.
Manas The lower mind, one of Antahkarana's four components — the part that registers sense data and flickers between options, before any real discernment happens.
Buddhi The discerning intellect, one of Antahkarana's four components — the part that actually judges and decides, one step up from Manas.
Annamaya (Kosha) The "food sheath" — the physical body itself, the most outer and dense of the traditional five layers (koshas) said to wrap the true Self. Not just a label: the Chandogya Upanishad traces this body to three elemental strands — fire, water, earth — interwoven in everything, including you, each refining through three grades. Solid food's coarsest residue is faeces, its middle grade is flesh, its finest is mind. Water's coarsest is urine, its middle is blood, its finest is breath. Fire's coarsest is bone, its middle is marrow, its finest is voice. Compressed to one line: the mind is made of food, the breath is made of water, the voice is made of heat.
Asanaya (Hunger) Water leading food along inside the body — the Upanishads' own etymology for hunger, built from a root meaning "to lead" or "to carry" (the same root behind gonaya, "a leader of cows"). Hunger, on this reading, is not an alarm bell but one element quietly moving another.
Udanya (Thirst) Fire evaporating water inside the body — the structural twin of Asanaya. What's left over once fire finishes with water gets a name of its own: heat, the residue neither element claimed.
Svapiti (Sleep) Sleep's own Sanskrit verb, traditionally glossed as sva apitah — "he enters himself." Not biological shutdown on this reading, but a forced nightly return: the waking mind, worn out from circling the external world in search of somewhere final to rest, finds nothing out there and is driven back into its own root.
Prana Vital, life-giving energy carried on the breath — not the breath itself (the physical inhale/exhale), and not Pranamaya, the subtler “sheath” it is said to constitute. In this framework, Prana is what gives the raw intake of air its rhythmic meaning at Layer 2: Breath.
Apana The downward and outward current among the five vayus: elimination, generation, exhalation, letting go. The Prashna Upanishad seats it in the organs of excretion and generation; later Hatha Yoga treats it as the counterweight to Prana, the pair to be balanced.
Samana The balancing current among the five vayus, seated in the middle of the body. In the Prashna Upanishad it equalizes what is taken in; the same digestive fire Layer 1 runs on.
Vyana The pervasive current among the five vayus: it moves through the whole body at once, along the nadis that the Prashna Upanishad says spring from the heart, distributing what the other four do locally.
Udana The upward current among the five vayus: it rises through the throat and carries speech and growth upward. Traditionally it is also what carries consciousness out of the body at death — a teaching of the tradition, not something this framework rests on.
Pranamaya (Kosha) The "breath/vital-energy sheath" — one layer in from the physical body: the layer of life-force, circulation, and breath that animates it.
Svasthya Sanskrit: sva (self) + stha (established/abiding) — Ayurveda's own word for health. Not the absence of disease; literally "abiding in one's own self."
Dosha Sanskrit: one of three biological energies in Ayurveda — Vata, Pitta, Kapha — patterns of function that govern body and mind. Distinct from the three gunas, which describe qualities of mind-nature.
Vata Dosha of Air and Ether. Governs movement, breath, and the nervous system. Dry, light, cold, rough, mobile. Balanced: creativity and flexibility; imbalanced: anxiety and dry skin.
Pitta Dosha of Fire and Water. Governs digestion, metabolism, and body temperature. Hot, sharp, light, oily, liquid. Balanced: intelligence and strong digestion; imbalanced: anger and inflammation.
Kapha Dosha of Earth and Water. Governs structure, immunity, and body fluids. Heavy, slow, cool, oily, stable. Balanced: calmness and strength; imbalanced: lethargy and weight gain.
Ayurveda Sanskrit: ayus (life) + veda (knowledge) — the science of life, where “life” is multidimensional: physical, emotional, mental, spiritual. Its premise is that health needs knowledge of the individual and their environment, not a one-size-fits-all remedy.
Agni Sanskrit: fire. In Ayurveda, the digestive and transforming fire — responsible for metabolism, absorption, and mental processing of food, emotion, and experience alike. (Also the fire element elsewhere on this site.)
Ama Sanskrit: undigested, raw. The residue of poor digestion — unprocessed food or unresolved emotion — felt as heaviness, toxicity, and stagnation.
Prakriti (constitution) An individual’s baseline constitution in Ayurveda — the proportion of Vata, Pitta and Kapha the tradition holds you start with. Not the Samkhya sense of “nature itself.”
Vikriti Sanskrit: altered. In Ayurveda, the current state of the doshas as they stand now, as distinct from the baseline (Prakriti).
Dhatu Sanskrit: that which holds or supports. The seven tissues of classical Ayurveda — Rasa, Rakta, Mamsa, Meda, Asthi, Majja, Shukra — each said to be built from the one before.
Shat Kriya Kala Sanskrit: the six stages of opportunity. The classical account of how a disturbance progresses from accumulation to a settled condition, with each stage a chance to intervene.
Srotas Sanskrit: channels or streams. The body’s transit networks in Ayurveda, along which food, breath, fluids, tissue and waste move. Charaka lists nadi among its synonyms; the yogic Nadi is a later, different use.
Samkhya Sanskrit, “enumeration.” One of the six classical schools of Indian philosophy. It describes reality as pure awareness (Purusha) and nature (Prakriti) unfolding through the three gunas into mind, body and elements — the groundwork Ayurveda draws on.
Vedanta Sanskrit, “the end of the Vedas.” The school of Vedic philosophy built on the Upanishads. It reads suffering as mistaken identity — taking yourself to be the body and mind — and liberation as recognizing the Self.
Gita (Bhagavad Gita) The Bhagavad Gita, a dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna set within the Mahabharata. References like (14.5) mean chapter 14, verse 5. Not the Ashtavakra Gita glossed elsewhere on this site.
Yoga Sanskrit, from yuj (to yoke or join). In this framework, the classical eight-limbed practice built around breath, posture, and concentration — not the studio stretching class the word usually means in English.
Tejas The subtle fire in Ayurveda — the quality of attention that transforms food, emotion and ideas, and, in balance, guards ojas; too much can burn it away. Not to be confused with the elemental “tejas” in Sanatkumara’s ladder.
Vyadhi Illness or bodily disturbance — already named earlier as the first of Patanjali’s nine obstacles to practice.
Anadhija Illness not generated by mental agitation — infection, injury, contagion, anything arriving from outside the mind.
Adhija Illness generated by Adhi, mental agitation — the psychosomatic branch, traced stage by stage in “How a Thought Becomes an Ulcer.”
Sara The essential or constitutional subtype of Adhija Vyadhi — deep-rooted, present from early on.
Samanya The ordinary subtype of Adhija Vyadhi — manufactured by everyday stress rather than constitution.
Ajeernatvam Under-digestion — too little energy to process food, leaving it stagnant.
Atijeernatvam Over-digestion — hyperactive energy burning through nourishment too quickly.
Kujeernatvam Wrong digestion — chaotic energy digesting irregularly, generating toxins.
Vishama Sanskrit: uneven or irregular. The unstable state of agni — strong one hour, weak the next — with gas, erratic digestion and anxious restlessness. Vata’s tendency.
Anupana The carrier a remedy is taken with — honey, ghee, milk, warm water — chosen because it changes where the medicine acts.
Sushruta Classical Indian physician, traditionally credited with the Sushruta Samhita, the foundational Ayurvedic text on surgery. The six-stage account of disease on this card comes from his tradition.
Charaka Classical Indian physician, traditionally credited with the Charaka Samhita, the foundational Ayurvedic text on internal medicine. The channels (srotas) on this card are described there.
Sharangdhara Samhita A classical Ayurvedic compendium from roughly the 13th century (samhita means “collection”). One of the classical sources for the five basic preparation forms laid out below.
Ojas Sanskrit: vigor. The refined result of clean digestion; felt as radiance, resilience, and a rested mind. The opposite outcome to Ama.
Artha Sanskrit: meaning, object, wealth. Two uses on this site: the object of the senses (Katha map), and prosperity — the second of the four Purusharthas, holding knowledge, health, contentment, and material wealth.
Purusharthas Sanskrit: the four aims of human life — Dharma (values), Artha (wealth), Kama (desire), Moksha (liberation). Not to be confused with Purushartha as self-effort in the Destiny section.
Tantra Literally "to weave." In classical Sanskrit usage, a governing system, model, or instructional treatise. In esoteric tradition, texts and practices that weave energy, ritual, and philosophy together, treating the universe as one interconnected web rather than something to renounce.
Puraka Inhalation — drawing breath in, traditionally done through the nose, evenly and without strain.
Kumbhaka Retention — suspending the breath, on either side of the inhale or exhale.
Rechaka Exhalation — releasing breath out, traditionally paced slower than or equal to the inhale.
Nadi A channel the traditional physiology maps subtle energy moving through — not a nerve in the anatomical sense, though the two get compared. In Charaka’s classical lists, nadi is also a synonym for srotas, the body’s transit channels; the yogic sense here is a later use of the word.
Ida The left-side channel in Hatha Yoga physiology, associated with the cooling, lunar current.
Pingala The right-side channel in Hatha Yoga physiology, associated with the heating, solar current.
Sushumna The central channel in Hatha Yoga physiology, said to run along the spine — the one Ida and Pingala are meant to balance into.
Marma Ayurveda's term for a point on the body where muscle, vessels, ligaments, bone and joint meet, and where life-force is said to gather — treated as a place the subtle and the physical share a single junction, rather than as two separate systems laid on top of each other.
Manomaya (Kosha) The "mind sheath" — the layer of thought, emotion, and sensory processing; where most people spend nearly all their time without noticing it's a layer at all.
Vijnanamaya (Kosha) The "wisdom/intellect sheath" — the layer of discernment and insight, one step subtler than ordinary thought: the part that can actually notice the mind sheath working.
Anandamaya (Kosha) The "bliss sheath" — the innermost and subtlest of the five, closer to the Self than to the intellect. Not a mood you generate, but what's left when nothing else is being generated. Doesn't correspond to its own row in the 7-layer matrix above — it sits just inside Layer 4 (Vijnanamaya), wrapping directly around Layer 7 (Atman).
Sat Being — that which does not come and go. One of the three faces of Satchitananda; used as a test, not a mood: does it still hold by Monday morning?
Chit Consciousness — that which does not grow stale with repetition. One of the three faces of Satchitananda; used as a test, not a mood: is the tenth time as alive as the first?
Ananda (quality) Bliss — that which needs nothing added to feel complete. One of the three faces of Satchitananda; used as a test, not a mood: does it ever feel like enough, on its own? (Distinct from Anandamaya Kosha above, the sheath this quality is named for.)
Samanvaya Harmony — reconciling every scriptural text so they all point to one non-dual reality, rather than contradicting each other. The first of the four chapters of the Brahma Sutras, which Shankaracharya's Bhasya follows.
Avirodha Non-Conflict — dismantling opposing theories through logic rather than by asserting louder. The second of the four chapters of the Brahma Sutras.
Sadhana Spiritual practice — the discipline that turns understanding into lived realization. The third of the four chapters of the Brahma Sutras.
Phala Result — not a reward added on top, but liberation actually lived out, not merely believed. The fourth and final chapter of the Brahma Sutras.
Yogic & Sanskrit Concepts
TermDefinition
Vritti A fluctuation or wave of the mind-stuff (Chitta) — the constant stream of mental chatter, images, and fleeting concepts stirred up by the senses, rippling across an otherwise still lake of awareness.
Nirodha Stilling, or restraint — the word Patanjali uses in Yoga Sutra 1.2 to define yoga itself: the stilling of the mind's fluctuations (Vritti).
Bhava Sanskrit: state of being, feeling. Here, the felt, energetic weight a thought or state carries — nostalgia clinging to a memory, anxiety clinging to the future. Not the thought itself, but the charge riding on it.
Purusha Pure consciousness, in Samkhya and Yoga philosophy — unmoving, unchanging, the witness that never itself becomes an object. Not a mixture with Prakriti, but what watches Prakriti happen.
Prakriti Nature itself, in Samkhya and Yoga philosophy — everything that changes, moves, and evolves: matter, mind, thought, and emotion, as distinct from the still consciousness (Purusha) observing it.
Tattvas Sanskrit for “thatnesses” or principles — the 24 building blocks of a manifest being as counted in this framework: 4 Antahkarana (Manas, Buddhi, Ahamkara, Chitta), 5 Pranas (vital airs), 5 Jnanendriyas (senses of perception), 5 Karmendriyas (organs of action), and 5 Mahabhutas (gross elements). Samkhya’s own 24 are counted differently: Prakriti, Mahat, Ahamkara, Manas, the five senses, the five organs of action, the five Tanmatras and the five Mahabhutas — with Purusha as the 25th.
Lokas Sanskrit for “worlds” or “planes” — the traditional 14-level cosmology of dimensional bandwidth. 7 Upper Lokas ascend toward expansion: Bhu, Bhuvar, Svar, Mahar, Jana, Tapa, Satya. 7 Lower Lokas descend toward contraction: Atala, Vitala, Sutala, Talatala, Mahatala, Rasatala, Patala — with the earth plane (Bhuloka) sitting at the pivot between them.
Abhyasa Sustained, uninterrupted practice, applied over a long stretch of time — the effort side of steadying the mind, paired with Vairagya as its counterpart.
Vairagya Dispassion, or non-attachment — not the absence of desire, but the absence of thirst for what desire promises. A finished taste, not a suppressed one.
Pratibhasika The apparent order of reality — purely subjective, cancelled the moment its private condition ends. Dreams, mirages, mistaking a rope for a snake.
Vyavaharika The transactional order of reality — shared, consistent, governed by cause and effect. The body, the world, daily life. Real for every practical purpose without being the final ground.
Paramarthika The absolute order of reality — unsublated in past, present, or future. What the transactional and apparent orders turn out to have been resting on all along.
Arambhavada The theory that God creates the world from separate material, the way a potter shapes a pot from clay. Rejected in Advaita — it puts creator and creation on separate sides.
Parinamavada The theory that a cause physically transforms into its effect, the way milk becomes yogurt. Rejected in Advaita — it would mean the changeless ground actually changes.
Vivartavada The theory that an effect is only an apparent form of its cause, the cause itself undergoing no change — a rope only appearing as a snake. Advaita's account of how the One appears as the many.
Upadhi A limiting adjunct — something that appears to divide or qualify a substance without changing what that substance is. A clay pot doesn't add anything to the space inside it; it only appears to enclose some.
Pratyaksha Direct perception — the five senses contacting an object. The foundation of empirical science; requires an object, which is exactly what it can't supply for the Self.
Anumana Inference — logic and deduction from a known relationship, such as inferring fire from smoke. Needs a shared mark between two things to compare; the Self has no second thing to compare against.
Shabda Testimony — specifically the Vedic texts, held in this tradition to be free of the ordinary defects of a human author. The only one of the three traditional means of knowledge that doesn't require an object.
Tat Tvam Asi “That thou art” — one of the four traditional Mahavakyas equating the individual (Jiva) with the absolute (Ishvara). Resolved by setting aside what conflicts between the two and keeping what's common to both.
Avidya Literally "not-knowing" — the root ignorance that mistakes the temporary, changing self for the true, unchanging one. The starting condition every path of self-enquiry works to dissolve.
Adhyasa Superimposition — mistaking the attributes of one thing for those of another, the way dim light lets a rope be mistaken for a snake. In the Samsara cycle, the attributes of a limited body-mind get superimposed onto the limitless Self.
Raga-Dvesha Attraction and aversion — the paired reflex of reaching for what seems to complete a felt lack, and recoiling from what threatens it, once that lack has been mistaken for who you are.
Phalam The fruit or result of an action — including the subtle residue (Vasana) it leaves behind, independent of whether the action succeeded at its stated aim.
Vasana A subtle latent tendency or impression, left behind by past thought and action, that inclines the mind toward repeating the same pattern.
Samsara Bandhanam The "bondage of Samsara" — the five-step engine (Avidya → Adhyasa → Raga-Dvesha → Karma → Phalam) that manufactures the felt sense of incompleteness and then feeds its own result back into step one.
Sadhana Chatushtaya The "four means of practice" — the traditional set of qualifications (Viveka, Vairagya, Shatsampatti, Mumukshutvam) said to prepare a mind for Vedantic inquiry, without which the teaching has nothing to take hold of.
Viveka Discrimination — the capacity to tell the eternal (Nitya) from the ephemeral (Anitya), the changeless from the changing. The bedrock qualification the other three are built on top of.
Nitya The eternal — what does not come and go, was not born and does not end.
Anitya The ephemeral — whatever begins, changes, and ends, however long the timescale.
Shatsampatti Literally "the six treasures" — a set of six inner disciplines (Shama, Dama, Uparati, Titiksha, Shraddha, Samadhana), traditionally grouped between Vairagya and Mumukshutvam, that stabilize the mind for inquiry.
Shama Mastery of the mind — the ability to keep it from chasing every stray thought or craving.
Dama Mastery of the senses — the ability to keep the sense organs from running the show.
Uparati Withdrawal from unnecessary external activity — not idleness, but the freeing-up of attention that constant busyness otherwise consumes.
Titiksha Forbearance — the capacity to endure the unavoidable pairs of opposites (heat/cold, praise/blame) without agitation or complaint.
Shraddha Faith — provisional trust in the teacher and the teaching, held long enough to actually test it, not blind belief held instead of testing it.
Samadhana One-pointed concentration — the capacity to hold attention steady on the inquiry itself, rather than letting it scatter.
Mumukshutvam The burning desire for liberation — not curiosity about liberation, but the same intensity of wanting normally reserved for survival. The spark the first three qualifications exist to give something dry to land on.
Neti Neti Sanskrit for "not this, not this" — the Upanishadic method of negation, systematically ruling out every object of experience as a candidate for the true Self, until only the un-negatable witness remains.
Gunas The three fundamental qualities that make up all of Prakriti (nature) — Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas. Every object, thought, mood, and meal is some shifting mixture of the three; not moral categories, but the raw material personality and matter are both built from. The word literally means “strand” or “cord”: the three strands the tradition says bind the embodied self.
Moha Delusion — the basic clouding of judgment that mistakes the false for the real. The functional end-state of unchecked conditioning left to run in the dark.
Vipallasa Pali (Sanskrit viparyāsa) — a perceptual distortion in Buddhist psychology — seeing the impermanent as permanent, the impure as pure, the painful as pleasurable, the not-self as self.
Sattva One of the three Gunas — the quality of lightness, clarity, and spiritual luminosity in Prakriti. The mind is calm enough here to see what's actually there, undistorted by craving (Rajas) or dulled by inertia (Tamas) — the condition under which self-knowledge becomes possible.
Rajas One of the three Gunas — the quality of energy, passion, and ceaseless movement. In balance: motivation, creativity, sustained effort. Out of balance: restlessness, anxiety, and desire-driven action. The indispensable bridge between Tamas and Sattva — without Rajas, nothing moves.
Tamas One of the three Gunas — the quality of heaviness, inertia, and darkness. In balance: necessary rest, grounding, timely sleep. Out of balance: dullness, confusion, and resistance to change. The heaviest of the three — and the starting point every ascent toward Sattva begins from.
Samskara A subconscious impression left behind by a past thought, emotion, or action, which conditions future thought and behavior — the mechanism behind habit, and behind Karma. The same word is also used, in a different sense, for the sixteen traditional rites of passage that mark a life (conception, initiation, marriage, and so on). One meaning is an inner imprint; the other is a ceremony.
Nirvana The Buddhist term for the extinguishing of the fires of craving, aversion, and delusion — release from the cycle of suffering, often used interchangeably with Moksha across traditions.
Dharma One's right action or duty in a given moment — not a fixed rulebook handed down from outside, but what is actually called for by your nature, circumstance, and stage on the path.
Tapas Disciplined effort — voluntary austerity and sustained practice, accepting friction now for a result that only steadiness can produce. One of the four laws of dharma alongside Satya, Yajña, and Daan.
Daan Giving — sharing what one has (resources, time, knowledge) with others as a standing habit, not an occasional gesture. One of the four laws of dharma alongside Satya, Tapas, and Yajña.
Svadhyaya Self-study — reading the texts and turning them on yourself, with teaching what you have learned counted as part of it (Taittiriya 1.9). Patanjali lists it in Kriya Yoga (Yoga Sutra II.1) beside tapas and surrender.
Santosha Contentment — one of the Niyamas in Patanjali’s eight limbs. Accepting what is, without needing it to be otherwise. A real virtue, and for that reason one of the places a practitioner can stall: contentment that turns into the belief of being finished is complacency.
Atmastuti Sanskrit for “praising oneself” — taking delight in one’s own spiritual progress until the progress itself becomes the thing being served. The third step in The Higher Climb.
Smriti-bhramsha Loss of memory — in the Gita (2.63), the stage where the person forgets their own purpose and values. In Karna’s story, the moment the knowledge goes missing exactly when it is needed.
Atithi Devo Bhava “The guest is a god” — the Taittiriya Upanishad’s formula for hospitality, held without conditions. See The Common Food.
Kama Desire — wish, longing, or sensory pleasure; one of the four traditional aims of life (Purusharthas) alongside duty, prosperity, and liberation. In this framework, the raw craving that hardens into a constructed identity (Ahamkara).
Karma The law of cause and effect applied to action and intention — every deed, thought, and reaction leaves an imprint (Samskara) that shapes what comes next.
Samsara The wheel of birth, death, and rebirth — the ceaseless, cyclical churn of conditioned existence every layer below the Self remains bound to. Not chaos in the sense of meaningless disorder, but the spinning, tension-filled dance every unliberated thing is caught inside, until Moksha or Nirvana breaks the cycle.
Moksha Liberation — release from the cycle of rebirth and from mistaken identity with the small self. The Vedantic term for the same recognition Buddhism calls Nirvana.
Yama The outward restraints — non-harming, truthfulness, non-stealing — first limb of Patanjali's Ashtanga Yoga, governing how you act toward others.
Niyama The inward observances — contentment, purity, discipline — second limb of Ashtanga Yoga, governing how you treat yourself.
Asana Posture, third limb of Ashtanga Yoga — traditionally just a seat stable enough to let the body be forgotten.
Pranayama Control of the breath, fourth limb of Ashtanga Yoga — not breathing exercises for their own sake, but the deliberate use of breath to steady the mind that rides on it.
Pratyahara Withdrawal of the senses from their objects, fifth limb of Ashtanga Yoga — the hinge between the outer four limbs and the inner three, where attention stops chasing the senses and turns inward.
Ekagrata One-pointedness — the literal quality Dharana, the sixth limb, trains the mind toward.
Dharana Single-pointed concentration — the sixth limb of Patanjali's Ashtanga Yoga. Binding the mind-stuff (Chitta) onto one object, on purpose, against its habit of scattering. Effortful by nature — the deliberate work that makes Dhyana possible.
Dhyana Sustained, uninterrupted meditative flow — the seventh limb, and the natural evolution of Dharana. The effort of "trying to focus" dissolves; what remains is an unbroken stream of attention toward the object. The bridge between concentration and Samadhi.
Kaivalya Literally “aloneness” — the final state in the Yoga Sutras, in which the Gunas fold back into their source (Sutra IV.34) and consciousness stands in its own nature. The field is not destroyed; it remains for everyone else (Sutra II.22). Not loneliness: wholeness, with nothing missing and nothing sought from another.
Dharma-megha Samadhi The “cloud of virtue” (Yoga Sutra IV.29) — the last samadhi in Patanjali’s arc, where goodness becomes the only thing present and is said to rain down like nectar, absorbing everything negative into itself.
Dukha Suffering, or more precisely unsatisfactoriness: the low-grade dis-ease of a mind that keeps expecting the next acquisition to settle it. The five Kleshas are the tradition’s account of its cause.
Klesa An affliction. Patanjali names five: Avidya (ignorance), Asmita (ego), Raga (attachment), Dvesha (aversion) and Abhinivesha (fear of death). Sutra IV.30 says they end together with karma.
Mala Literally “dirt” — the specific impurities of desire (Kama), anger (Krodha) and greed (Lobha), distinct from Avarana, the veil of ignorance covering consciousness. Both lift together in Sutra IV.31.
Kritartha Literally “one whose purpose is done.” Said of the Gunas once they have finished giving the spirit its training in experience (Sutra IV.32); from there they withdraw into their causes.
Samapatti Yoga Sutra I.41 — the mutual commingling of knower, knowing and known, so that the three no longer stand apart as separate things.
Jivanmukti Liberation while the body is still alive — freedom lived out in this life, not postponed to after it. The one who has it is a Jivanmukta.
Videhamukti Liberation after the body falls — freedom that remains once there is no body left to live it in. The Kaivalya Upanishad treats Kaivalya as covering both this and Jivanmukti.
The Inconscient In Sri Aurobindo’s system, the state of Consciousness-Force so completely absorbed in its own forms (Matter) that it appears to know nothing, not even itself. Not a separate insentient substance, and not an illusion — a total, willed self-forgetting.
The Subliminal Self The layer of being that sits behind the Inconscient’s forgetting rather than past it — aware, awake, and self-remembering even while the surface appears unconscious. Named in Aurobindo’s Four Mechanisms of Cognition and Sevenfold Ignorance.
Samadhi The state in which the external form of an object of meditation is given up entirely and only its essential meaning remains — absorption without separation between observer and observed.
Cosmic Consciousness In Maharishi Mahesh Yogi’s scheme, the fifth state of consciousness — Turiya, except it no longer disappears once waking, dreaming, or sleep resume. The witness stays present through all activity, not only in meditation.
God Consciousness In Maharishi Mahesh Yogi’s scheme, the sixth state of consciousness — the same unbroken witnessing from Cosmic Consciousness, paired with perception refined enough to register the subtlest layer of whatever is perceived.
Unity Consciousness In Maharishi Mahesh Yogi’s scheme, the seventh and final state of consciousness — every object keeps its own shape and boundary, but is directly experienced as the same Self doing the perceiving.
Tarka Standard reasoning, debate, and analysis, in the Shiva Sutras' scheme of logic — useful, but it shifts every time a new fact arrives.
Kutarka Fault-finding aimed at good intentions and twisted purely to win an argument — the Shiva Sutras' “wrong logic,” which breeds paranoia, destruction, and ignorance.
Vitarka Thought without the need to win anything — the Shiva Sutras' “special logic,” asking unanswerable questions like “Who am I?” that exhaust the ego and open onto Self-knowledge.
Jnanam Bandhah A Shiva Sutra: limited knowledge itself creates bondage — the instant something is called “known,” its living, changing range narrows to fit a fixed, past-based definition.
Vismayo Yoga Bhumikah A Shiva Sutra: wonder is the foundation for union — knowledge held with amazement stays open; knowledge held as settled certainty closes the door to reality.
Aviveko Maya Sausuptam A Shiva Sutra: lack of discrimination is like deep sleep — failing to tell the passing (opinion, reputation) apart from the real is itself a kind of unconsciousness.
Nartaka Atma / Rango’ntaratma A Shiva Sutra: the Self is the dancer, the inner Self is the stage — reversing the usual sense of scale. The world doesn't contain you; you contain the stage it plays out on.
Shakti Chakra Sandhane Vishvasamharah A Shiva Sutra: focusing on the energy centers dissolves the illusory world — sustained attention on the body's energy centers is what loosens Maya's grip.
Chittam Mantrah A Shiva Sutra: the mind becomes the mantra — whatever sound or thought the mind repeats is what it eventually turns into.
The Seven Chakras
TermDefinition
Chakra Sanskrit for “wheel” — one of the body’s psychic energy centers in the yogic and tantric traditions, traditionally mapped along the spine from base to crown. This framework borrows the seven-chakra ladder as a map for how consciousness itself matures, using each chakra as a different operating altitude of awareness rather than a location to unblock.
Root Chakra (Muladhara) The base of the ladder — operating on the consciousness of physical survival, material form, and biology. In this framework it governs Layer 1: Body, from the first claiming of physical space in the womb to the body’s return to the earth at death.
Sacral Chakra (Svadhisthana) Operating on the consciousness of life-force, emotional baseline, and vital rhythm. In this framework it governs Layer 2: Breath, from the first cry that floods the lungs with air to the last exhalation that dissolves individual life-force back into the atmosphere.
Solar Plexus Chakra (Manipura) Operating on the consciousness of linear logic, everyday perception, and sensory processing. In this framework it governs Layer 3: Mind, from a newborn’s first overwhelming sensory input to the fading of the senses at the end of life.
Heart Chakra (Anahata) Operating on the consciousness of structural truth, objective logic, and core beliefs. In this framework it governs Layer 4: Intellect, from a child’s first curiosity about existence to an elder’s lifetime of wisdom offered forward as a kind of art.
Throat Chakra (Vishuddha) Operating on the consciousness of systemic patterns, karma, and personal history. In this framework it governs Layer 5: Memory, from a person’s first impression to the eventual erasure of ego-memory into the collective unconscious.
Third Eye Chakra (Ajna) Operating on the consciousness of individual identity, self-will, and personal archetype. In this framework it governs Layer 6: Ego, from a toddler’s first sense that “I am separate” to the eventual dissolution of that separate self.
Crown Chakra (Sahasrara) The summit of the ladder — operating on the highest consciousness of the Eternal Witness, unity, and absolute transcendence. In this framework it governs Layer 7: Self / Soul, the one layer said to stand entirely outside time, birth, and death.
The Four States (AUM)
TermDefinition
AUM The primal sound-symbol of Vedanta, mapped here to the four states of consciousness: A is Jagrat (waking), U is Svapna (dreaming), M is Prajna (deep sleep) — and the silence after the sound stops is Turiya, the awareness underneath all three. Taittiriya 1.8 adds its everyday work: the word of assent (“yes, so be it”), the opening of a chant, the permission to make an offering, and the vow-word of someone setting out to reach Brahman.
Jagrat The ordinary waking state — consciousness engaged with the external, physical world through the senses.
Svapna The dream state — consciousness turned inward, generating its own world out of memory and imagination while the body rests.
Prajna Deep, dreamless sleep — no object of any kind, waking or dream, yet not nothing: you wake up and know you slept well, which means something was present to know it.
Turiya The "fourth" state — not another state alongside waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, but the constant awareness present underneath all three, witnessing each without changing when they change.
Vishva Waking consciousness bound to a single body — the individual counterpart to Virat, the same state at cosmic, unbound scale.
Taijasa Dream consciousness bound to a single sleeping body — the individual counterpart to Hiranyagarbha, the same state at cosmic scale.
Ishvara Deep sleep at cosmic scale — the individual counterpart is Prajna. Not ignorance of the world, but the causal stillness everything else rests on.
Virat The physical cosmic manifestation — the universe itself, considered as a single body. The cosmic counterpart to Vishva.
Hiranyagarbha Literally the "golden womb" — the universal "I-Am," pure self-consciousness arising before any physical form exists. The cosmic counterpart to Taijasa.
Alchemical Stages
TermDefinition
Lead (Base Matter) The heaviest, most inert starting material in alchemy — the raw, unrefined condition everything else in the sequence works on.
Copper (Purification) An early refining stage — impurities in the base material start burning off, but the result is still volatile and unstable.
Iron (Strength) A hardening stage — the volatility of the previous stage sets into something rigid and load-bearing, for better and worse.
Silver (Refinement) A polishing stage — the rigid material of the last stage gets refined into something more responsive and reflective, without yet reaching gold's stability.
Gold (Illumination) The classical alchemical goal-material — incorruptible, stable, "illuminated." What the earlier, cruder stages were always in service of becoming.
Quintessence Literally the "fifth essence" — beyond the four classical elements (earth, water, air, fire), the pure spirit or vital essence said to underlie and animate all of them.
Philosopher’s Stone The legendary end-goal of alchemy — not a literal object but a completed transformation, capable of "turning lead into gold": in this framework, base conditioning fully transmuted into realized SELF.
The Seven Hermetic Principles
TermDefinition
Mentalism "The All is Mind." The principle that the universe is fundamentally mental in nature — matter as a mode of mind, not the other way around.
Correspondence "As above, so below." The principle that the same patterns repeat at every scale — a single moment of reaction contains the same structure as a lifetime's conditioning.
Vibration "Nothing rests; everything moves." The principle that all matter, energy, thought, and spirit are in constant motion — stillness is always relative, never absolute.
Polarity "Everything is dual; opposites are identical in nature, differing only in degree." Hot and cold are the same phenomenon, temperature, at different points — not two separate things.
Rhythm "Everything flows, out and in; everything has its tides." The principle that all things swing between poles in a measurable rhythm — including moods, motivation, and insight.
Cause & Effect "Every cause has its effect; every effect has its cause." Nothing happens by pure chance — what looks random is usually a cause operating on a plane you haven't traced yet.
Gender "Gender is in everything." Not biological sex — a generative/receptive polarity present in all creation, thought, and action, the interplay that produces anything new.
Theosophy & Subtle Bodies
TermDefinition
Thought-Form In the clairvoyant taxonomy of Annie Besant and C.W. Leadbeater (1901), the second, detachable effect of every thought — a floating form built of astral matter, coloured by the thought's quality and shaped by its nature, that travels until it discharges its energy on a mind vibrating in sympathy with it. See The Pain-Body for a modern description of the same basic mechanism.
Kama-Manas The lower, desire-driven mind — Manas (thought) fused with Kama (desire/passion) — identified in Theosophy as the animating charge inside a thought-form. Compare Manas above.
Astral Plane / Astral Body The subtler layer of substance, in this and related traditions, said to sit just beyond ordinary matter — the medium a thought-form is built from and travels through, and the vehicle through which emotion is felt.
(Artificial) Elemental This tradition's term for a thought-form once it is complete — a temporary, semi-autonomous entity with an outer shell of quickened elemental essence wrapped around the thinker's own mental energy as its core.
“Not-Self” (Naming Note) Human Design — a separate modern system for self-knowledge, built by combining astrology, the I Ching, and chakra theory — uses this exact phrase for energy that isn't native to a person but runs through them anyway and gets mistaken for identity. Noted here only because it lands close to how this site uses SELF — as a prompt to ask what's actually running the moment, not the moment itself. The two systems aren't otherwise connected; this isn't an endorsement of Human Design's wider framework.
Brainwave & Awareness States
TermDefinition
Delta (0.5–4 Hz) The slowest brainwave band, dominant in deep, dreamless sleep — the conscious mind is fully offline while the body repairs itself.
Theta (4–8 Hz) Active during the twilight zone between waking and sleep, or deep meditation — attention turns inward toward imagery, intuition, and dreams.
Alpha (8–12 Hz) The state of calm, relaxed wakefulness — an "idling" visual system, often peaking when the eyes close and the mind drifts.
Mu (8–13 Hz) Shares Alpha's frequency but sits over the motor cortex — the body idling in neutral, present during physical stillness and vanishing the instant you move, or even intend to.
Beta (12–30 Hz) The everyday waking state — dominant when attention is directed outward: solving problems, conversing, making decisions.
Gamma (30–100 Hz) The fastest standard brainwave band, associated with binding information across brain regions into one coherent experience — present during peak focus and sudden insight. See the research note →
Lambda (100+ Hz) A rarely-observed, very high frequency band associated with profound meditative or altered states — deep stillness paired with rapid, high-coherence processing.
Clinical & Scientific
TermDefinition
Senescence The point where cells stop dividing and repairing themselves as efficiently — the biological beginning of decline, before outright breakdown. On the Master Matrix, this is the stage between Aging and Mortality at every layer above the body too, from the Mind's Fatigue to the Ego's Rigidity.
Information Integration A measure of how much different regions of the brain are combining what they're processing into one unified picture, rather than just being separately active. See the research note →
